# Overview

cppDE generates and compiles per-model C++ code for three related
problems through three entry points that share a common R interface:
\texttt{cppODE()}, \texttt{cvode()}, and \texttt{cppFUN()}.
Table \ref{tab:entry-points} summarises their scope.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l l @{}}
\toprule
                           & \texttt{cppODE()}                & \texttt{cvode()}              & \texttt{cppFUN()}             \\
\midrule
Problem class              & ODE                              & ODE                           & algebraic $y = g(x, p)$       \\
Methods                    & \texttt{bdf, adams, rb4, tsit5}  & \texttt{bdf, adams}           &                             \\
First-order sensitivities  & in-tree dual-number AD           & SUNDIALS, generated JVP       & dual AD                       \\
Reverse-mode gradient      & yes (discrete adjoint)           & yes (CVODES ASA)              & yes (generated VJP)           \\
Second-order sensitivities & yes (nested duals, fwd-over-rev) & no                            & yes (nested duals)            \\
External dependencies      & LAPACK; KLU optional             & SUNDIALS $\ge 6.0$; KLU opt.  & none                          \\
Codegen                    & graph AD + \texttt{R CMD SHLIB}  & graph AD + \texttt{R CMD SHLIB} & graph AD + \texttt{R CMD SHLIB} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\caption{The three cppDE entry points and what they cover. The
codegen pipeline of Section \ref{sec:codegen} (parse the user's
expressions into an expression graph, differentiate on the graph, emit
C++, compile via \texttt{R CMD SHLIB}, load via \texttt{dyn.load}) is
shared, as is the \texttt{solveODE()} dispatcher used by both
integrator backends.}
\label{tab:entry-points}
\end{table}

The integrator entry points \texttt{cppODE()} and \texttt{cvode()}
expose the same R-side interface: the user supplies named character
vectors of right-hand sides together with optional events, forcings,
and parameter vectors, and the returned model handle is passed to
\texttt{solveODE()}. The two backends differ only in the numerical
core. \texttt{cppODE()} emits a self-contained C++ source that
includes the headers under \texttt{inst/include/cppde/}; the
resulting binary depends on LAPACK and, optionally, KLU.
\texttt{cvode()} emits a thin glue layer that links against the
system-installed SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES library and inherits its
numerical behaviour.

Section \ref{sec:codegen} describes the code generator the three
entry points share. Section \ref{sec:cppde} describes the in-tree integrator
\texttt{cppODE()}: its four time-stepping methods, forward-mode
automatic differentiation for parameter sensitivities, the reverse-mode
discrete adjoint, whose cost does not depend on the number of
parameters, and the transport of sensitivities across events.
Section \ref{sec:cvode} describes the SUNDIALS-backed
\texttt{cvode()} integrator and its adjoint sensitivity analysis.
Section \ref{sec:funcpp} describes \texttt{cppFUN()}, which compiles
algebraic maps $y = g(x, p)$ with their first and second derivatives
and no time integration, typically observation maps and
reparametrisations $p = \Phi(\theta)$. Section
\ref{sec:bench} benchmarks the two integrator backends against each
other on $43$ problems, and the reverse and second-order modes against
their forward counterparts.

# Code generation \label{sec:codegen}

Every entry point turns the user's expressions into straight-line C++
templated over the scalar type, so that one source serves the value,
the dual-number and the nested-dual instantiation. The derivatives the
integrators need beyond that, namely the Jacobian, the contractions of
the discrete adjoint, and the time derivatives of the right-hand side
and of the event roots, are formed at code-generation time by automatic
differentiation on an expression graph.

\textbf{Expression graph.} Each expression is read by Python's own
parser and lowered into a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are
hash-consed: a node is identified by its operation, its operands and
its constant attributes, and is created at most once. A subexpression
that occurs several times is therefore a single node, without a
separate elimination pass. Sums and products are kept
flat with numeric coefficients and exponents, and numeric constants
are normalised so that equal values map to equal nodes. Syntax the
parser does not read is passed to SymPy and translated into the same
graph; SymPy also supplies the derivative of a function the graph has
no rule for.

\textbf{Derivatives.} A forward sweep over the graph forms a
Jacobian-vector product, a reverse sweep a vector-Jacobian product;
both add nodes to the same graph, so derivative and value share their
common parts. The Jacobian $J = \partial f/\partial x$ is assembled in
one of two ways. By entries, each state-dependent node carries the
sparse gradient of its value with respect to the states, and the
gradients of the roots are the nonzero entries of $J$. The work of
this accumulation is
$W_{\mathrm{ent}} = \sum_{v} |\mathrm{supp}\,\nabla v|$, summed over
the $E_s$ state-dependent nodes $v$ of $f$. Entries are used while
$W_{\mathrm{ent}} \le \max(4E_s, 50\,000)$. Beyond that, a greedy
distance-2 colouring of the column intersection graph groups
structurally orthogonal columns, and if it needs at most $n_x/4$
colours, one Jacobian-vector product per colour, seeded with ones on
the columns of that colour, recovers all entries of those columns;
otherwise entries are kept. The reverse contractions
$J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and $(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$
are vector-Jacobian products, and the derivatives the Rosenbrock
stages and the event localisation require are Jacobian-vector products
along $\dot x = f$. A single forward or reverse sweep costs time linear
in the size of the graph. The entry accumulation costs
$W_{\mathrm{ent}}$, which grows with the density of $J$, and the
colouring path costs one sweep per colour.

\textbf{Linear tables.} A sum of at least twelve terms
$c_j\,x_j\,\varphi$ with numeric $c_j$ and a common state-free factor
$\varphi$ becomes a row of a constant matrix $C$, so that
$f(x) = \phi(x, Cx)$. The generated code evaluates $z = Cx$ once per
call from a sparse or dense table, and assembles the Jacobian as
\begin{equation}
  J = \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z}\,C,
  \label{eq:linmap-jacobian}
\end{equation}
while the reverse contractions apply $C^{\mathsf T}$. A dense coupling,
such as a dipolar interaction among all states, then costs a table
rather than a sum of expressions per entry.

\textbf{Loops.} A method-of-lines discretisation repeats the same
statement for every grid point. Statements whose graphs agree up to
state indices and constants form a class; a class of at least sixteen
instances is emitted as one loop over index and constant tables, and a
sum of many terms of one structure as an inner loop. Differentiation
remains per instance, so the work of the generator grows with the
number of instances, while the size of the emitted code for a regular
model does not.

# \texttt{cppODE()} \label{sec:cppde}

## Initial value problem and four methods

This section describes the in-tree integrator of \texttt{cppODE()}:
the four time-stepping methods, their step-size control and dense
output, forward sensitivities through dual numbers, time- and
root-triggered events, and the reverse mode. The coefficients of each
method are listed in Appendices \ref{app:bdf-coeffs} to
\ref{app:tsit5-coeffs}.

The initial-value problem solved by \texttt{cppODE()} is
\begin{equation}
  \dot{x}  = f\bigl(x,\, p_{\mathrm{dyn}},\, t\bigr),
  \qquad x(t_0) = p_{\mathrm{init}},
  \label{eq:ivp}
\end{equation}
with state $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ and parameter vector
$p = (p_{\mathrm{init}}, p_{\mathrm{dyn}})$ collecting the initial
conditions and the dynamic parameters. The right-hand side $f$ may
depend explicitly on time, in which case the system is
non-autonomous; an explicit time argument is also necessary for the
forcing-function machinery used to inject time-dependent inputs. The
Jacobian of $f$ with respect to the state is denoted
$J = \partial f / \partial x$ throughout.

## Stiffness and the choice of method

Stability is analysed on the linear test equation
$\dot y = \lambda y$ with $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^-$, whose exact
solution decays. A one-step method applied to it multiplies $y$ by an
amplification factor $R(z)$ per step, $z = h \lambda$. The method is
\emph{A-stable} if $|R(z)| \le 1$ on the entire left half-plane, so
that the numerical solution decays whenever the exact one does, for
any step size; \emph{A($\alpha$)-stable} if the same bound holds on
the wedge $\{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |\arg(-z)| \le \alpha \}$ for some
angle $\alpha < 90^{\circ}$; and \emph{L-stable} if it is A-stable
and $R(z) \to 0$ as $\operatorname{Re}(z) \to -\infty$, which damps
very stiff transients within one step.

The initial-value problem \eqref{eq:ivp} is \emph{stiff} on
$[t_0, t_{\mathrm{end}}]$ when an explicit method has to take steps
much smaller than local accuracy demands, to keep the products
$h \lambda_k$ inside its stability domain, where $\{\lambda_k\}$ are
the eigenvalues of $J$ along the trajectory. Stiffness therefore
depends on the spectrum of $J$, on the integration horizon, and on the
requested tolerance. Chemical-kinetics networks with rate constants
spanning several orders of magnitude are stiff in this sense, as are
many discretised parabolic PDEs.

BDF/NDF and Rosenbrock4 have stability domains that contain the left
half-plane or a wide wedge of it and are suited to stiff problems;
Adams-Moulton and Tsit5 are not, whatever the tolerance. The cost of a
wrong choice is asymmetric: an explicit method on a stiff problem fails
or is driven to uneconomic step sizes, while an implicit method on a
non-stiff problem pays a constant overhead per step. BDF/NDF is
therefore the default when the spectrum of $J$ is unknown, and for a
large model with a sparse Jacobian it runs on the sparse linear solver
(\texttt{sparse = TRUE}).

## Multistep methods

Linear multistep methods build the solution at the new time step
$x_n$ from a linear combination of the most recent $k+1$ states
and right-hand-side values, $\{x_{n-j}, f_{n-j}\}_{j=0}^{k}$. Reusing
earlier steps, they attain high accuracy with few right-hand-side
evaluations per step.

cppDE implements the BDF and the Adams families in the Nordsieck
representation used throughout SUNDIALS [@hindmarsh2005sundials].
Instead of the past $k+1$ states it stores the \emph{scaled derivative
array}
\[
  z_n =\left(x_n,\, h_n \dot{x}_n,\, \dfrac{h_n^2}{2!} \ddot{x}_n,
                  \,\dots,\,
                  \dfrac{h_n^{k}}{k!} x_n^{(k)} \right),
\]
the value at the current time and its first $k$ derivatives, each
scaled by the matching power of the step size. A change of step size
or order is then a linear transformation of $z_n$ rather than a refit
through past data.

### Backward Differentiation Formula ($\mathtt{bdf}$)

The BDF formula of order $q$ defines $x_n$ implicitly by the
condition
\begin{equation}
  \sum_{j=0}^{q} \alpha_j\, x_{n-j} \;=\; h_n\, f(x_n, t_n),
  \label{eq:bdf}
\end{equation}
which is exact whenever $x(t)$ is a polynomial of degree at most
$q$ on the past $q+1$ nodes. The method is A-stable for $q \le 2$
and A($\alpha$)-stable for $q \in \{3,4,5\}$; the stability angle
$\alpha$ shrinks monotonically from $86^\circ$ at $q=3$ to
$51^\circ$ at $q=5$.

The implicit corrector \eqref{eq:bdf} is solved by Newton iteration,
\begin{equation}
  W \Delta x^{(\nu)} = - \tilde r \left(x_n^{(\nu)}\right),
  \qquad
  x_n^{(\nu+1)} = x_n^{(\nu)} + \Delta x^{(\nu)},
  \label{eq:newton}
\end{equation}
with leading coefficient $\beta_0 = 1/\alpha_0$ and the iteration
matrix
\begin{equation}
  W = \frac{1}{h_n\, \beta_0}\symbb{1} - J\bigl(x_n^{(\nu)}, t_n\bigr),
  \label{eq:bdf-W}
\end{equation}
in the form adopted by SUNDIALS [@hindmarsh2005sundials], which
differs from the textbook expression $I - h_n \beta_0\, J$ by the
scalar factor $h_n \beta_0$. The factorisation of $W$ is the dominant
cost of a step and is reused across steps, as described below.

The default in cppDE is the Numerical Differentiation Formula (NDF)
variant of @MATLABODESuite, which adds a correction proportional to
the Nordsieck predictor error to the BDF corrector,
\begin{equation}
\sum_{m=1}^{q} \dfrac{1}{m}\, \nabla^{m} x_n - h_n f(x_n, t_n) - \kappa_q\, \gamma_q\, \left(x_n - x_n^{\mathrm{pred}}\right) = 0, \qquad \gamma_q  = \sum_{m=1}^{q} \dfrac{1}{m}, \label{eq:ndf}
\end{equation}
where $\nabla$ denotes the backward-difference operator. The
modification scales $\beta_0$ in \eqref{eq:newton} by $(1 - \kappa_q)$
and multiplies the leading truncation-error coefficient $1/(q+1)$ by
$1 + \kappa_q (q+1) \gamma_q$. With $\kappa_q < 0$ the truncation
error at a fixed step size decreases, which permits a larger step at
the same accuracy. The values of $\kappa_q$ are tabulated in Appendix
\ref{app:bdf-coeffs}; they give the step-size gains over classical BDF
reported by @MATLABODESuite, $26\,\%$ for $q \le 3$ and $12\,\%$ for
$q = 4$, at a small reduction in stability angle. Setting
\texttt{useNDF = FALSE} recovers the classical BDF formulas
($\kappa_q \equiv 0$).

The corrector takes at most three iterations, each with one
right-hand-side evaluation and one linear solve. It converges when
the damped correction norm $\delta\,\min(1, \rho)/\tau_q \le 1$, where
$\delta$ is the WRMS norm of the latest correction, $\rho$ the estimated
contraction rate and $\tau_q$ an order-dependent constant. As in
CVODE, $W$ is refactorised when $\gamma = h_n\beta_0$ has moved by more
than $30\,\%$ since the last factorisation, after $20$ steps, or after a
failed corrector; the Jacobian itself is re-evaluated after $51$ steps
or when a failure is attributed to it. A sparse $W$ then changes only
on its diagonal. BDF/NDF is the default method in cppDE.

### Adams-Moulton in PECE form ($\mathtt{adams}$)

The Adams-Moulton family integrates the local interpolant of $f$
over $[t_{n-1}, t_n]$. Writing $f$ as the unique polynomial through
the $q+1$ samples $\{(t_{n-j}, f_{n-j})\}_{j=0}^{q}$ and integrating
gives
\begin{equation}
  x_n \;=\; x_{n-1} \;+\; h_n \sum_{j=0}^{q} \beta_j\,
            f(x_{n-j}, t_{n-j}),
  \label{eq:adams}
\end{equation}
which is implicit in $x_n$ through the $j=0$ term. cppDE solves the
corrector by fixed-point iteration in predict-evaluate-correct-evaluate
(PECE) form, without a Jacobian or a linear solve. The Nordsieck
predictor supplies $x_n^{P}$, the right-hand side is evaluated there,
and \eqref{eq:adams} is applied with $f(x_n^{P}, t_n)$ in place of
$f(x_n, t_n)$. If the correction has not converged, the evaluation and
the correction are repeated, at most three times in all, as in CVODE.
A step that converges on the first correction costs two right-hand-side
evaluations.

The Adams-Moulton stability domain on the negative real axis
shrinks rapidly with order; for $q \ge 3$ it contains no wedge of
$\mathbb{C}^-$, so the method is unsuitable for stiff problems. For
non-stiff problems with smooth solutions and a long integration
horizon, its maximum order $q_{\max} = 12$ and two right-hand-side
evaluations per step make it competitive with explicit Runge-Kutta
methods of fixed order.

## Single-step methods

Single-step methods carry no information beyond the current state
and reach order $p > 1$ through internal stages. Both methods below
therefore restart after an event at full order, whereas the multistep
methods rebuild the Nordsieck history from order $1$.

### Rosenbrock ($\mathtt{rb4}$)

A Rosenbrock method of $s$ stages with diagonal coefficient $\gamma$
linearises the implicit Runge-Kutta condition about $(x_n, t_n)$ and
defines stage values $k_i$ by
\begin{equation}
  W k_i = f\left(x_n + \sum_{j<i} \alpha_{ij}\, k_j,\,
                 t_n + c_i\, h_n \right) + \dfrac{1}{h_n} \sum_{j<i} \dfrac{\gamma_{ij}}{\gamma}\, k_j + h_n\, d_i\, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x_n, t_n),
  \label{eq:rosenbrock-stage}
\end{equation}
with the iteration matrix
\begin{equation}
  W = \frac{1}{\gamma\, h_n}\symbb{1} - J(x_n, t_n).
  \label{eq:rosenbrock-W}
\end{equation}
The method coefficients are listed in Table \ref{tab:rosenbrock-coeffs}.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$\alpha_{ij}$ & weights with which stage $i$ combines all earlier stages $k_j$, $j<i$ \\
$c_i$         & time abscissa of stage $i$ inside the step, with $c_i = \sum_{j<i}\alpha_{ij}$ \\
$\gamma_{ij}$ & weights with which the linear-solve correction at stage $i$ uses earlier stages \\
$\gamma$      & common diagonal coefficient appearing in the iteration matrix $W$ \\
$d_i$         & weights that pick up the explicit time dependence of $f$ via $\partial f/\partial t$ \\
$m_i$         & weights combining the stages into the advanced solution $x_{n+1}$ \\
$\hat{m}_i$   & weights combining the stages into the embedded order-3 estimator used for step control \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Rosenbrock method coefficients.}
\label{tab:rosenbrock-coeffs}
\end{table}

The advanced solution and embedded error estimate are
\[
  x_{n+1} = x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} m_i\, k_i,
  \qquad
  \hat{x}_{n+1} \;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} \hat{m}_i\, k_i.
\]
Each stage \eqref{eq:rosenbrock-stage} is a single linear solve, with
no Newton iteration. Per accepted step cppDE evaluates $J$ and
factorises $W$ once, performs five right-hand-side evaluations, and
back-substitutes six times.

cppDE uses the order-$4$ coefficients of @hairer2010solving
[§IV.7], the same set as the \texttt{rosenbrock4} stepper of
Boost.Numeric.Odeint. The pair is L-stable and carries an embedded
order-$3$ estimator. Dense output uses an order-$3$ interpolant built
from the stage values $k_i$ and the coefficient sets $d_i^{(2)}$ and
$d_i^{(3)}$ of Appendix \ref{app:ros-coeffs}.

Rosenbrock methods are competitive with BDF on stiff problems whose
Jacobian is cheap relative to the right-hand side, and they restart
after an event without rebuilding an order. Rosenbrock4 is the stiff
method of choice for systems with frequent state discontinuities at
moderate state dimension.

### Tsitouras ($\mathtt{tsit5}$)

Tsitouras is the explicit Runge-Kutta pair of order $5(4)$ derived
by @TSITOURAS2011770 under the first column simplifying assumption alone,
\[
  \sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i\, a_{ij} \;=\; b_j\,(1 - c_j),
  \qquad j = 1, \dots, s,
\]
without the row simplifying assumption
$\sum_{j} a_{ij}\, c_j = c_i^2/2$, $i \ge 3$, on which the
Dormand-Prince pair rests. Dropping the row condition leaves free
parameters, which Tsitouras spends on a smaller leading-error norm;
the coefficients of Appendix \ref{app:tsit5-coeffs} satisfy the column
condition to rounding and violate the row condition. The pair has $s = 7$ stages
with the First-Same-As-Last (FSAL) property,
\[
  k_7 \;=\; f(x_{n+1},\, t_n + h_n)
       \;=\; k_1 \text{ at step } n+1,
\]
so an accepted step costs six right-hand-side evaluations rather
than seven. The method coefficients are listed in Table \ref{tab:tsit5-coeffs}.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$a_{ij}$    & weights with which stage $i$ combines earlier stages (strictly lower triangular) \\
$c_i$       & time abscissa of stage $i$ inside the step, with $c_i = \sum_{j<i} a_{ij}$ \\
$b_i$       & weights combining the stages into the advanced order-5 solution; $b_7 = 0$ \\
$\hat{b}_i$ & weights combining the stages into the embedded order-4 estimator; $\hat{b}_7 \ne 0$ \\
$k_i$       & right-hand side at stage $i$: $k_i = f\!\left(x_n + h_n\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}k_j,\; t_n + c_i h_n\right)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Tsit5 method coefficients.}
\label{tab:tsit5-coeffs}
\end{table}

The advanced solution and embedded error estimate are
\[
  x_{n+1} = x_n + h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} b_i\, k_i,
  \qquad
  \hat{x}_{n+1} = x_n + h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} \hat{b}_i\, k_i,
\]
and the local error estimate used for step-size control is
\[
  e_{n+1} = h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} (\hat{b}_i - b_i)\, k_i.
\]
Dense output uses the step endpoints and their derivatives
$(f_n, f_{n+1}) = (k_1, k_7)$, which the FSAL property already holds.

Tsit5 needs no Jacobian and no linear solve, and of the four methods it
advances furthest per right-hand-side evaluation. It suits non-stiff
problems whose right-hand side is expensive to evaluate.

## Adaptive step-size control

The error estimate $e_n$ delivered by each method is reduced to a
scalar through the weighted root-mean-square norm
\begin{equation}
  \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} =
  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_x} \sum_{j=1}^{n_x} \left(
    \frac{e_{n,j}}{w_{n,j}}
  \right)^{\!2}},
  \qquad
  w_{n,j} = \mathtt{atol} + \mathtt{rtol}\,|x^{\mathrm{ref}}_{n,j}|,
  \label{eq:wrms}
\end{equation}
in which $w_{n,j}$ is a per-component tolerance combining an
absolute floor $\mathtt{atol}$ and a relative scale
$\mathtt{rtol}\,|x^{\mathrm{ref}}_{n,j}|$, so that components of
different magnitude and unit enter on a common scale. The reference
state $x^{\mathrm{ref}}_n$ that enters the relative term is the
accepted solution $|x_n|$ at the start of the step in BDF/NDF and
Adams, as in CVODE, so the weights are fixed for the whole step,
and the component-wise maximum $\max(|x_n|, |x_{n+1}|)$ in the
single-step methods. A step is accepted when
$\| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} \le 1$.

The single-step methods select the next step size with the
proportional-integral (PI) controller of @hairer2010solving. Write
$\varepsilon_n = \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}$ and let $p$ be the order
of the embedded error estimate, $p = 3$ for Rosenbrock4 and $p = 4$ for
Tsit5. After an accepted step
\[
  h_{n+1} = h_n\, \min\Bigl\{\rho_{\max},\; \max\Bigl(\rho_{\min},\;
        S\, \varepsilon_n^{-(\alpha+\beta)}\,
        \varepsilon_{n-1}^{\,\beta}\Bigr)\Bigr\},
  \qquad
  \alpha = \frac{0.7}{p+1}, \quad \beta = \frac{0.4}{p+1},
\]
with $S = 0.9$, $\rho_{\min} = 0.2$, $\rho_{\max} = 5$, and
$\varepsilon_{n-1}$ the norm of the previous accepted step, floored at
$0.01$. On the first step and after a rejection the integral form
$S\,\varepsilon_n^{-1/(p+1)}$ replaces the PI factor, and after a
rejection the factor is further capped at $1$. A rejected step is
retried with the factor $S\,\varepsilon_n^{-1/(p+1)}$ clamped to
$[\rho_{\min}, 0.9]$.

The multistep methods select step size and order as CVODE does. With
$d_{q'}$ the WRMS norm of the error estimate at order $q'$, the
candidate ratios are
\[
  \eta_{q'} = \frac{1}{\bigl(B_{q'}\, d_{q'}\bigr)^{1/(q'+1)} + 10^{-6}},
  \qquad q' \in \{q-1,\, q,\, q+1\},
\]
with $B_{q-1} = B_q = 6$ and $B_{q+1} = 10$. The neighbouring orders
are compared $q+1$ steps after a change to order $q$ and every second
step while the order is unchanged, and the largest ratio fixes the
next order. A ratio below $1.5$ leaves $h$ unchanged,
and the ratio is capped at $10^4$ on the first step and at $10$
afterwards.

### The first step

The first step has no previous error norm. cppDE estimates it from the
initial state as in @hairer2008solving, Algorithm II.4.4: a rough
$h_0 \sim \|x_0\| / \|f_0\|$ fixes a scale, a second derivative
$\ddot x$ along the trajectory fixes the curvature, and
\begin{equation}
  h_1 = \left(
    \frac{0.01}{\max\bigl(\|f_0\|, \|\ddot x\|\bigr)}
  \right)^{\!1/(p+1)}
  \label{eq:hnw-h1}
\end{equation}
turns the two into a step for a method of order $p$. The implicit
methods obtain $\ddot x = \partial f/\partial t + J f$ from the
generated Jacobian, the explicit one from a finite difference of
$f$. All norms are the weighted norms of \eqref{eq:wrms}; with
\texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} they include the sensitivity components.

Two bounds follow, in the form CVODE uses. An upper bound keeps a
single Euler step from changing any component by more than a
fraction of its own scale, and is capped by the remaining interval;
a lower bound keeps $h_0$ above the rounding of the time variable.
The multistep methods use a port of the CVODES routine
\texttt{cvHin}, which refines $\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{lb}} h_{\mathrm{ub}}}$
by a finite-difference curvature until two successive estimates agree
within a factor of two, so the first step equals the one CVODES takes
on the same problem. The estimator runs again after every event, on
the post-event state.

## Dense output

User-requested output times do not in general coincide with the
adaptive step grid produced by the controller. Each accepted step
therefore carries a local interpolant that allows evaluation of
$x(t)$ at any time inside that step at the cost of polynomial
arithmetic only, and no right-hand-side evaluation. With
$s = (t - t_n)/h_n \in [0, 1]$ the three families use:

- Tsit5: the cubic Hermite interpolant through $x_n$, $x_{n+1}$ and the
  FSAL derivatives $k_1$, $k_7$,
  \[
    x(t) = (1+2s)(1-s)^2\, x_n + s^2(3-2s)\, x_{n+1}
         + s(1-s)^2\, h_n k_1 + s^2(s-1)\, h_n k_7 .
  \]
- Rosenbrock4: the stage-based cubic of @hairer2010solving,
  \[
    x(t) = (1-s)\, x_n + s\bigl(x_{n+1} + (1-s)(c_3 + s\, c_4)\bigr),
    \qquad
    c_3 = \sum_{i=1}^{5} d_i^{(2)} k_i, \quad
    c_4 = \sum_{i=1}^{5} d_i^{(3)} k_i,
  \]
  with the coefficients of Table \ref{tab:ros-dense}.
- BDF/NDF and Adams: the Nordsieck polynomial of degree $q$ held after
  the step, $x(t) = \sum_{j=0}^{q} z_{n+1,j}\,
  \bigl((t - t_{n+1})/h_n\bigr)^{j}$.

Both single-step interpolants are of order $3$, below the order of the
step itself ($5$ for Tsit5, $4$ for Rosenbrock4); the multistep
interpolant has the order $q$ of the step.

## Forward sensitivities

### Dual-number arithmetic

Parameter sensitivities of the trajectory are computed by forward-mode
automatic differentiation rather than by finite differences, whose
truncation and round-off errors need several integrations to control.
Forward-mode AD augments every floating-point scalar with a component
that carries its directional derivative. Arithmetic operations and
elementary functions are overloaded for the augmented type, and the
C++ source that evaluates $f$ is compiled unchanged for both the
primal and the sensitivity computation.

The augmented type is the \emph{dual number}
\[
  \tilde x = x + x'\,\varepsilon,
  \qquad \varepsilon^2 = 0,\quad \varepsilon \ne 0,
\]
where $x \in \mathbb{R}$ is the primal value and $x' \in \mathbb{R}$
is the directional derivative. Reading $\tilde x$ as the first two
terms of a Taylor expansion in $\varepsilon$, the arithmetic follows
from the rules of calculus: for $\tilde x = x + x'\varepsilon$ and
$\tilde y = y + y'\varepsilon$,
\[
  \tilde x + \tilde y = (x+y) + (x'+y')\varepsilon,
  \qquad
  \tilde x \cdot \tilde y = xy + (xy' + x'y)\varepsilon,
\]
and for any smooth scalar function $g$,
\[
  g(\tilde x) = g(x) + g'(x)\,x'\,\varepsilon.
\]
A composition of these operations carries the derivative of the
composed function, so the source that evaluates $f$ over $\mathbb{R}$
returns $f$ and its directional derivative when called with dual
inputs.

### Tangent storage

A dual carries its value inline and $m$ tangent slots behind a pointer,
and $m$ is $\mathrm{ncol}$ of the tangent, read at run time rather
than fixed at compile time. The tangents of temporaries come from a
thread-local bump arena, whose allocations since the start of a generated
model body are released in one operation when that body returns. The
state vectors the stepper keeps across steps instead point into one
contiguous $n_x \times m$ block per vector, the tangent slab, sized once
per solve. A parameter set wider than one call should hold is answered in
blocks of directions; since the step sequence of a tangent-blind solve
does not depend on $m$, the blocks share one grid and the assembled
Hessian equals a single pass exactly.

A dual whose width has never been set has no slots, and reading a tangent
from it yields zero. Buffers that are zeroed before use, such as the
cotangents of a backward sweep, therefore have their width declared
first; otherwise their derivatives would be structurally zero.

### Sensitivity equations via dual evaluation

Let the ODE right-hand side depend on a parameter vector
$p \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p}$,
\[
  \dot x = f(x, p, t), \qquad x(t_0) = x_0(p),
\]
and define the \emph{sensitivity matrix}
\[
  S_p = \frac{\partial x}{\partial p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times n_p},
  \qquad
  (S_p)_{ij} = \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}.
\]
Seeding each state component with its row of $S_p$ gives the
dual-valued state vector
\[
  \tilde x_i = x_i + (S_p)_{ij}\,\varepsilon_j,
\]
where $\varepsilon_j$ is the dual unit associated with direction $p_j$
and summation over $j$ is implied. Evaluating $f$ component-wise
over the dual algebra and collecting the $\varepsilon_j$-coefficient
of the $i$-th output gives
\[
  \bigl[f(\tilde x, p, t)\bigr]_{i,\,\varepsilon_j}
  = \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_k}\,(S_p)_{kj}
    + \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial p_j},
\]
where repeated $k$ is summed. Since the primal part of the dual
evaluation recovers $\dot x_i = f_i(x,p,t)$, differentiating
$\dot x_i = f_i$ with respect to $p_j$ and identifying the
$\varepsilon_j$-coefficient with $\dot{(S_p)}_{ij}$ yields
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_p
    = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,S_p
      + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p},
  \qquad
  S_p(t_0) = \frac{\partial x_0}{\partial p}.
  \label{eq:sensitivity-p}
\end{equation}
One dual evaluation of $f$ therefore yields the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} for all columns of $S_p$, at a cost
proportional to $n_p$ and without forming $\partial f/\partial x$.

### Seeding: from $S_p$ to $S_\theta$

The parameters of inference are often not the entries of $p$ but a
vector $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^M$ to which the dynamic parameters
$p_{\mathrm{dyn}}$ and the initial condition
$x_0 = p_{\mathrm{init}}(\theta)$ are linked through a
reparametrisation $p = \Phi(\theta)$. The quantity of interest is then
\[
  S_\theta = \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}
           \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times M},
\]
related to $S_p$ by the chain rule
$S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial\theta$. Substituting this
relation into \eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} yields the evolution equation
for $S_\theta$ directly,
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_\theta
    = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,S_\theta
      + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_{\mathrm{dyn}}}
        \,\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta},
  \qquad
  S_\theta(t_0) = \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{init}}}{\partial \theta}.
  \label{eq:sensitivity-theta}
\end{equation}
The matrix $\partial p / \partial\theta$ is the \emph{tangent} of the
inputs, supplied through the \texttt{tangent} argument of
\texttt{solveODE()} and fixed for the integration. The choice
$\partial p/\partial\theta = I_{n_p}$ gives $S_\theta = S_p$; any
other choice propagates $M$ directions of $\theta$-space at the cost
of $M$ additional state vectors.

### Error norm with sensitivities

With forward sensitivities the integrator carries
$S_\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x \times M}$ beside the state, and every
step produces $1+M$ error vectors of length $n_x$: the state estimate
$e_n^{(x)}$ and one estimate $e_S^{(k)}$ for each column
$\partial x/\partial \theta_k$. cppDE combines them by the maximum of
the per-vector WRMS norms, as CVODES does, rather than by a flat WRMS
over all $n_x(1+M)$ components.

The state norm $\| e_n^{(x)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}$ is exactly
\eqref{eq:wrms}. The sensitivity column norm is its analogue, with
$S_\theta$ replacing $x$ in both the error vector and the weight,
\begin{equation}
  \| e_S^{(k)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} =
  \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_x} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x} \left(
    \frac{(e_S)_{ik}}{w^{(k)}_{i}}
  \right)^{\!2}},
  \qquad
  w^{(k)}_{i} = \mathtt{atol} + \mathtt{rtol}\,|(S_\theta)_{ik}^{\mathrm{ref}}|,
  \label{eq:wrms-col}
\end{equation}
in which $(S_\theta)_{ik}^{\mathrm{ref}}$ is taken from the same
source as $x^{\mathrm{ref}}_n$: the accepted value for the multistep
methods, the maximum over both step ends for the single-step methods.
The step-size controller uses the largest of the state norm and the
$M$ column norms,
\begin{equation}
  \| e_n \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}} = \max\left\{
    \| e_n^{(x)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}},\;
    \max_{1 \le k \le M} \| e_S^{(k)} \|_{\mathrm{WRMS}}
  \right\}.
  \label{eq:wrms-sens}
\end{equation}

A flat WRMS divides by $n_x(1+M)$ and averages the squared errors over
the directions, so a large error in one column can be hidden by small
errors in the others. The maximum holds every direction to the
requested tolerance separately.

The corrector of BDF/NDF measures its corrections with the same
maximum, so a sensitivity direction that has not converged causes
further iterations or a smaller step even when the state has. With
\texttt{solveODE(..., sensErrCon = FALSE)} the error test, the order
selection, the corrector test and the initial-step estimates use the
state components only, and the step sequence is that of a value run.

## Events and restarts

cppDE supports two kinds of events that interrupt smooth
integration. A *time-triggered event* fires at a user-specified
time $t_e(\theta)$ that may depend on $\theta$ through a
closed-form expression. A *root-triggered event* fires when a
user-supplied event function $g_e(x, t)$ crosses zero along the
trajectory; the firing time $t^{*}(\theta)$ is then defined
implicitly by $g_e(x(t^{*}), t^{*}) = 0$. In both cases an event
applies a discontinuous reset to the state,
\[
  x^{+} = g(x^{-}, t),
\]
for example the dosing of a kinetic species, a clipping rule that
enforces non-negativity, or a switch between dynamical regimes.

### Restart cost

Single-step methods (Rosenbrock4, Tsit5) resume after the reset with a
full-order step. Multistep methods (BDF/NDF, Adams) restart at order
$1$ and rebuild the Nordsieck array over several steps, which dominates
the cost on problems with frequent events.

For every method the step size is re-estimated from the post-event
state, with the initial-step estimator of the solve and the remaining
interval as upper bound. For a single-step method this is the whole
restart.

### Sensitivity transport across a discontinuity

The reset map $g$ acts on the trajectory $x(t, \theta)$ at the firing
time $t^{*}(\theta)$. The naive update of the sensitivity, by the
linearisation of $g$ around the pre-event state,
$S_\theta^{+} = (\partial g/\partial x)\,S_\theta^{-}$, is incorrect
in the presence of an event because the firing time itself depends
on $\theta$. A perturbation $\delta t^{*}$ of the firing time induces
short integrations of $\dot x = f$ on either side of the event, with
$f$ taking different values before and after the reset. Denote by
$f^{-}$ the right-hand side just before the reset, evaluated at
$x^{-}$, and by $f^{+}$ the right-hand side just after the reset,
evaluated at $g(x^{-}, t^{*})$. The sensitivity at the first grid
time following the event then receives two contributions in
addition to the linearised reset:

1. \emph{Pre-event drift.} The pre-event trajectory $x^{-}$ flows
   along $\dot x = f^{-}$ from the grid time
   $t_*^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t^{*})$ to the $\theta$-perturbed
   firing time $t^{*}$, over a displacement
   $\delta t^{*} = t^{*} - t_*^{(0)}$ whose scalar part vanishes but
   whose $\theta$-derivatives do not.
2. \emph{Post-event drift.} The reset state $g(x^{-}, t^{*})$ then
   flows along $\dot x = f^{+}$ from $t^{*}$ back to the grid time
   over the negative of the same displacement.

Both shifts contribute terms of order
$f^{\pm}\,(\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta)$ to the sensitivity at the
grid time; to first order they give the \emph{saltation matrix} of
Section \ref{sec:saltation}.

cppDE replaces the bare reset by a sequence of forward drift, reset
and backward drift, evaluated in dual arithmetic. Each drift is one
step of Heun's method, the explicit trapezoidal rule, which averages
the right-hand side at both ends of the interval. Since
$\delta t^{*}$ has scalar part zero, the value of $x$ at the grid time
is unchanged and only the $\theta$-derivatives of the displacement
enter the state. The reset $g$ is applied between the drifts in the
same arithmetic, so its first and second derivatives enter as well.
Without sensitivities, $g$ is applied as an ordinary map.

Time-triggered and root-triggered events differ in how $\delta t$
enters: through the expression $t_e(\theta)$ in the first case, and
through the implicit function theorem applied to $g_e = 0$ in the
second.

### Time-triggered events

When the firing time is given as an expression $t_e(\theta)$, its
derivatives with respect to $\theta$ follow from the chain rule. The
integrator advances on the scalar grid time
$t_e^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t_e)$ and treats the displacement
\begin{equation}
  \delta t = t_e - t_e^{(0)},
  \qquad \mathrm{scalar}(\delta t) = 0,
  \label{eq:fixed-dt}
\end{equation}
as a dual number whose value is zero but whose first-order tangents
are $\partial t_e/\partial \theta_a$ and whose second-order tangents
are $\partial^2 t_e/\partial \theta_a \partial \theta_b$. The state at
the grid time $t_e^{(0)}$ is denoted $x^{-}$; its first-order tangents
are the pre-event sensitivities $S_\theta$.

The transport consists of a Heun step along $\dot x = f$ from
$t_e^{(0)}$ to $t_e$, the reset $g$ at $t_e$, and a Heun step back
from $t_e$ to $t_e^{(0)}$ with the post-event right-hand side,
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
  &\text{forward:}\quad
    f_1 = f(x^{-}, t_e^{(0)}), \quad
    x_E = x^{-} + f_1\,\delta t, \quad
    f_2 = f(x_E, t_e), \\
  &\hphantom{\text{forward:}\quad}
    x^{*} = x^{-} + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_1 + f_2)\,\delta t, \\
  &\text{reset:}\quad
    x^{*}_{+} = g(x^{*}, t_e), \\
  &\text{backward:}\quad
    \tilde f_1 = f(x^{*}_{+}, t_e), \quad
    x_B = x^{*}_{+} - \tilde f_1\,\delta t, \quad
    \tilde f_2 = f(x_B, t_e^{(0)}), \\
  &\hphantom{\text{backward:}\quad}
    x^{+} = x^{*}_{+} - \tfrac{1}{2}(\tilde f_1 + \tilde f_2)\,\delta t.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:fixed-heun}
\end{equation}
An Euler step would suffice for first-order sensitivities: since
$\mathrm{scalar}(\delta t) = 0$, the powers $\delta t^{k}$ for
$k \ge 2$ have no first-order dual content, and any
$O(\delta t^{2})$ term drops out of $\partial x^{+}/\partial \theta$.
At second order the curvature term
\[
  \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(J\,f + \partial f/\partial t\bigr)\,\delta t^{2},
  \qquad J = \partial f/\partial x,
\]
acquires a non-vanishing second-order dual component, because the
square of $\delta t$ has a non-zero mixed derivative
\[
  \frac{\partial^{2}(\delta t)^{2}}{\partial \theta_a\,\partial \theta_b}
    = 2\, \frac{\partial t_e}{\partial \theta_a}\,
          \frac{\partial t_e}{\partial \theta_b},
\]
although its value and first derivatives are zero. Heun's second
evaluation, at the shifted state and the shifted time $t_e$, supplies
this term and leaves a truncation error of $O(\delta t^{3})$. Evaluating
$f_2$ and $\tilde f_2$ at $t_e^{(0)}$ instead would drop the
$\tfrac{1}{2}(\partial f/\partial t)\,\delta t^{2}$ part for a
right-hand side that depends explicitly on time.

### Root-triggered events

For a root event the firing time $t^{*}(\theta)$ is defined
implicitly by
\begin{equation}
  G(t^{*}(\theta), \theta) :=
    g_e\bigl(x(t^{*}(\theta), \theta), t^{*}(\theta)\bigr) = 0.
  \label{eq:root-condition}
\end{equation}
The event is handled in three steps: localisation of $t^{*}$ on the
scalar trajectory, reconstruction of the dual residual $\delta t^{*}$
by the implicit function theorem, and the Heun transport
\eqref{eq:fixed-heun} of the time-triggered case.

#### Localisation

The integrator evaluates $g_e$ at the end of every accepted step and at
every requested output time. A crossing is accepted on
$[t_n, t_{n+1}]$ when the two readings have opposite signs, and also
when $g_e(x_{n+1}, t_{n+1})$ is exactly zero, as for a root on a
sampled time. A zero at the lower end is not a new crossing, since it
was reported with that sample; this also keeps an event from firing a
second time on the surface it has just been applied on, where $g_e$
is zero up to round-off.

The crossing is refined on the dense output of the accepted step,
without further right-hand-side evaluations. The iteration is a
false-position step whose interpolation factor is clamped to
$[0.1, 0.9]$, which bounds the stagnation of the classical rule and
keeps its speed on a nearly linear $g_e$. It stops when the bracket is
narrower than the root tolerance, after at most fifty iterations, or
when an iterate returns $g_e = 0$ exactly. It returns as
$t_*^{(0)} := \mathrm{scalar}(t^{*})$ the end of the final bracket
that still carries the sign $g_e$ had before the crossing. The
localisation says nothing about how $t^{*}$ depends on $\theta$, so
the dual residual $\delta t^{*} = t^{*} - t_*^{(0)}$ is reconstructed
from \eqref{eq:root-condition}.

#### Dual residual of the event time

If $G$ is smooth at the crossing and $\partial G/\partial t \neq 0$
there, the implicit function theorem gives the derivative of
$t^{*}(\theta)$ from $G(t^{*}, \theta) = 0$. Differentiating
\eqref{eq:root-condition} once with respect to $\theta$ and applying
the chain rule gives
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial \theta}
    = -\frac{G_\theta}{G_t}
    = -\frac{\nabla_x g_e \cdot S_\theta}
            {\nabla_x g_e \cdot f + \partial g_e/\partial t}\bigg|_{*},
  \label{eq:dt-star-first}
\end{equation}
in which the denominator is the total time derivative
$\dot g_e = \nabla_x g_e \cdot f + \partial g_e/\partial t$ along the
trajectory at the crossing. The condition $\dot g_e \neq 0$ means
that the trajectory crosses the event surface transversally; for a
grazing crossing the firing time is not differentiable in $\theta$,
and the fallback described under simultaneous events applies. In
dual-number form,
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first} is realised as the quotient
\begin{equation}
  \delta t^{*} = -\frac{g_e(x^{-}, t_*^{(0)})}
                       {\dot g_e(x^{-}, t_*^{(0)})},
  \label{eq:dt-star-quotient}
\end{equation}
where both $g_e$ and $\dot g_e$ are evaluated on the dual-typed
state $x^{-}$ at the scalar grid time. The generated partials
$\nabla_x g_e$ and $\partial g_e/\partial t$ are needed only for
$\dot g_e$; the dual arithmetic forms $\nabla_x g_e \cdot S_\theta$
in the numerator. The scalar value of the numerator, of the order of
the root tolerance, is set to zero before the division, so
$\delta t^{*}$ is zero in value and carries only derivatives.

The first-order part of \eqref{eq:dt-star-quotient} equals
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first}. At second order the quotient misses one
term, because $g_e$ is evaluated at the scalar time $t_*^{(0)}$ rather
than at the dual time $t^{*}$, so the $G_{tt}$ contribution from the
time argument of $g_e$ is absent. Expanding \eqref{eq:root-condition}
to second order in $\theta$ and matching coefficients gives it. Writing $\delta t^{*} = \delta t^{*}_{(1)} + \delta t^{*}_{(2)} + \cdots$
and using $G(t_*^{(0)}, \theta^{(0)}) = 0$,
\[
  0 = G_t\,\delta t^{*}_{(2)}
      + \tfrac{1}{2} G_{tt}\,(\delta t^{*}_{(1)})^{2}
      + G_{t\theta}\,\delta t^{*}_{(1)}\,\delta\theta
      + \tfrac{1}{2} G_{\theta\theta}\,\delta\theta^{2},
\]
of which the dual quotient supplies the $G_{t\theta}$- and
$G_{\theta\theta}$-contributions but not the $G_{tt}$-contribution.
The corrected update is therefore
\begin{equation}
  \delta t^{*} \leftarrow \delta t^{*}
    - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\frac{G_{tt}}{G_t}\,(\delta t^{*})^{2},
  \label{eq:dt-star-second}
\end{equation}
where
\[
  G_{tt} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d} t^{2}}
            g_e\bigl(x(t), t\bigr)\bigg|_{*}
\]
is the second total time derivative of $g_e$ along the trajectory.
cppDE supplies $G_{tt}$ from generated code or, where that is not
available, by a forward finite difference of $\dot g_e$. Equation
\eqref{eq:dt-star-second} changes only the second-order components of
$\delta t^{*}$.

With $\delta t^{*}$ known, the Heun transport \eqref{eq:fixed-heun}
carries $x^{-}$ across the event to the grid time $t_*^{(0)}$, with
$\delta t^{*}$ in place of $\delta t$ and $t_*^{(0)} + \delta t^{*}$
in place of $t_e$.

#### Simultaneous events

Two or more root conditions can cross zero within the same accepted
step. cppDE localises each crossing separately and groups those that
share $t_*^{(0)}$ within the localisation tolerance into a cluster.
For a cluster the forward Heun shift is taken once to the common event
surface, every triggered reset is applied there (the reset maps are
assumed to commute), and one backward shift returns the state to the
grid time, at four right-hand-side evaluations whatever the number of
events. The dual residual $\delta t^{*}$ is computed once, from the
first event in the cluster with non-zero $\dot g_e$, and shared by the
others, which sit at the same grid time with the same parameter
dependence through $x^{-}$.

If every event in the cluster has $\dot g_e = 0$ at the surface, the
denominator of \eqref{eq:dt-star-first} vanishes and the implicit
function theorem gives no $\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta$. cppDE
detects this case by the size of $|\dot g_e|$ and applies the reset as
a plain map without transport, which is exact in the limit where both
contributions $f^{\pm}\,(\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta)$ vanish.

#### Conditions switched by a reset

A reset is a jump, not a crossing of the continuous solution, so a
root condition that a reset makes true escapes the sign-change search.
cppDE therefore evaluates every condition on both sides of a jump. A
condition whose sign changes across the jump fires there, one per
sweep so that a reset can switch on the next condition; one that
already held before the jump does not fire again.

The switched resets are applied on the surface of the jump, between
the forward and the backward shift of the event that caused it,
rather than after the transport has returned to the grid time. One
Heun transport then carries the composition of both resets, and its
sensitivities, to both orders, equal those of the same reset written
as a time-triggered event at that time.

Terminal conditions are excluded from this path: they stop the
integration rather than reset a state.

### Connection to the saltation matrix \label{sec:saltation}

The classical treatment of sensitivity transport across a
discontinuity is the \emph{saltation matrix}, which adds to the reset
Jacobian $\partial g/\partial x$ a term for the $\theta$-dependence of
the firing time:
\[
  S_\theta^{+} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,S_\theta^{-}
    + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
             + \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,f^{-} - f^{+} \right)
       \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial \theta}.
\]
The first-order part of the Heun transport equals this expression,
for time-triggered events with
$\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta = \partial t_e/\partial \theta$ and for
root events with $\partial t^{*}/\partial \theta$ from
\eqref{eq:dt-star-first}. Unlike the saltation matrix, the transport
also yields the second-order sensitivities. It resides in
\texttt{cppde\_saltation.hpp}, the event loop in
\texttt{cppde\_event\_engine.hpp}.

## Reverse-mode sensitivities: the discrete adjoint \label{sec:reverse}

Forward sensitivities cost one additional state vector per direction
in $\theta$, so a gradient of a scalar objective over $M$ parameters
costs $M$ times the value alone. When the quantity of interest is a
single scalar $J$, a likelihood or a residual sum of squares, the
transpose of that computation delivers the whole gradient at a cost
independent of $M$. cppDE builds this mode with
\verb|cppODE(..., derivMode = "reverse")|.

The reverse mode computes a contraction rather than the sensitivity
matrix. Given a cotangent $W \in \mathbb{R}^{n_t \times n_x}$
attached to the observed trajectory, the reverse mode returns
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta_j
    = \sum_{o=1}^{n_t} \sum_{i=1}^{n_x}
      W_{oi} \,
      \frac{\partial x_i(t_o)}{\partial \theta_j},
  \qquad j = 1,\dots,n_x+n_p,
  \label{eq:adjoint-contraction}
\end{equation}
in one sweep. The row index $o$ runs over the observation times and the
column index $i$ over the state components. Write $w_o \in
\mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ for the vector formed from row $o$, the cotangent
attached to the trajectory at $t_o$. For a least-squares objective $W$
is the residual weighted by the error
model, and $\bar\theta$ is $\nabla_\theta J$ exactly. Several cotangents
may be supplied as columns of a three-dimensional array, one sweep
each.

### The adjoint equation

The contraction \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction} can be evaluated
without forming $S_p$. Both backends implement the classical
construction below, with different discretisations. Let $S_p$ be the
forward sensitivity of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-p}. Define
$\lambda(t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$ backwards from the end of the
observed interval by
\begin{equation}
  \dot\lambda = -J(x, p, t)^{\mathsf T}\lambda,
  \qquad \lambda(T^+) = 0,
  \qquad \lambda(t_o^-) = \lambda(t_o^+) + w_o,
  \label{eq:adjoint-ode}
\end{equation}
so that $\lambda$ evolves continuously between observation times and
jumps by the cotangent row at each one. Along the solution
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
    \left(\lambda^{\mathsf T} S_p\right)
    = -\lambda^{\mathsf T} J S_p
      + \lambda^{\mathsf T}\!
        \left(J S_p + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)
    = \lambda^{\mathsf T} \frac{\partial f}{\partial p},
  \label{eq:adjoint-identity}
\end{equation}
where the two Jacobian terms cancel, so $\lambda$ is defined without
reference to $\theta$. Integrating \eqref{eq:adjoint-identity} over $[t_0, T]$ and collecting
the jumps, whose contributions are exactly the terms of
\eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction}, gives
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta
    = \left(\frac{\partial x_0}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \lambda(t_0)
    + \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!
      \int_{t_0}^{T}
      \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
      \mathrm{d}t .
  \label{eq:adjoint-result}
\end{equation}
Taking $\theta$ to be the initial state and the parameters themselves
makes both outer factors identities and splits the answer in two,
\begin{equation}
  \bar x_0 = \lambda(t_0),
  \qquad
  \bar p = \int_{t_0}^{T}
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda(t)\,
    \mathrm{d}t,
  \label{eq:adjoint-quadrature}
\end{equation}
which is the pair a reverse solve reports. A reparametrisation
$p = \Phi(\theta)$ is applied afterwards through the outer factors of
\eqref{eq:adjoint-result}, the chain rule of
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta} applied on the left.

The gradient therefore costs one backward solve of a linear system of
dimension $n_x$ and a quadrature of dimension $n_p$, whatever $M$;
$\partial f/\partial p$ enters only through its contraction with
$\lambda$ and is never formed. The two parts of
\eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature} are returned stacked as the rows of the
\texttt{tangent} argument are indexed, states first and parameters second.

### Discrete and continuous adjoints

Equation \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} describes the exact trajectory. Two
discretisations of it are in common use, and cppDE provides both.

The \emph{continuous} adjoint differentiates first and discretises
afterwards: \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} is handed to an integrator of its
own and solved backwards over forward states recovered by
interpolation [@cao2003adjoint]. This is the route of CVODES, which
\texttt{cvode()} exposes (Section \ref{sec:asa}).

The \emph{discrete} adjoint reverses that order. It transposes the map
the forward run applied, one accepted step at a time, and is what
\texttt{cppODE()} implements. Both approximate the same gradient and
converge as the tolerance is lowered. They differ in three respects.

\textbf{Consistency of value and gradient.} The discrete adjoint
differentiates the trajectory that was actually computed, so it returns
the derivative of the value the forward run reported, up to rounding.
The continuous adjoint approximates the derivative of the exact
solution, which no run computes, so its gradient and the accompanying
value are consistent only to $O(\mathrm{tol})$. Tightening the backward
tolerance alone does not remove that difference.

\textbf{Discontinuities.} A jump in the state implies a jump in
$\lambda$, given by the transposed saltation matrix of the event. A
continuous adjoint has to restart its backward integration with that
matrix at every event. In the discrete adjoint the jump is the
transpose of arithmetic the forward run performed, handled like every
other step.

\textbf{Linear algebra per step.} The adjoint of an implicit step is a
single transposed solve against the iteration matrix of that step,
evaluated at the state stored in its checkpoint, without a Newton
iteration and without error control of its own. The continuous adjoint
integrates a stiff linear ODE instead, with its own step-size control
and step count.

### The step map and its adjoint

Reverse accumulation has no counterpart in an augmented arithmetic. A
dual number carries its derivative with its value, available as soon
as an operation has executed, whereas an adjoint is a sum over all
later uses of a quantity.

A step's adjoint can be obtained by recording its operations on a tape
and traversing the record backwards, or by writing it in closed form,
since the map is one accepted step of a known method on a fixed grid.
cppDE uses the closed form and keeps no tape.

An accepted step of the multistep family decomposes into three parts:
\begin{align}
  z^{\text{pred}} &= A\, z^{\text{in}}, \label{eq:step-pred}\\
  r(y, z^{\text{pred}}, \theta) &= 0, \label{eq:step-corr}\\
  z^{\text{out}} &= B\, z^{\text{pred}} + c\, a, \qquad a = y - z^{\text{pred}}_0,
  \label{eq:step-tail}
\end{align}
namely the Nordsieck rescale and Pascal shift, the corrector, and the
tail that the controller applies between the acceptance of this step and
that of the next. The operators $A$, $B$ and $c$ act on the slot index
only; their coefficients follow from the carry and are identical for
every state component. They are read off the stepper rather than
transposed by hand: a probe whose states are the Nordsieck slots is
driven through the routines the forward step runs, carrying the identity
in the $[\text{slot} \times \text{component}]$ array, and one pass
returns every column. The adjoint therefore uses exactly the
coefficients of the forward step.

The corrector is differentiated by the implicit function theorem. The
derivative $\partial r/\partial y$ is the iteration matrix
$W = I - \gamma J$ that the forward step factorises, so one transposed
solve against $W$ replaces the entire Newton iteration. For the
Rosenbrock family the corresponding object is a transposed stage
recursion, six solves against one factorisation; for an explicit method
it is the backward recursion over the tableau.

The contractions the adjoint requires are supplied by the model and
emitted by the code generator beside the right-hand side:
$J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$, $(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$
and, for a Rosenbrock method, the same two applied to $J v$, which
carries a second derivative because its stages solve against a matrix
built from the Jacobian.

### Checkpoint per step

The backward pass needs the states the forward run passed through.
They are stored as one checkpoint per accepted step, holding the
step-start state, the carry, the time, the step size, and a record of
the operations the controller applied to the carry afterwards. The
memory is linear in the number of steps and holds no derivatives.

The sweep re-forms and refactorises the iteration matrix at each
checkpoint, since the factorisations of the forward run are not kept.
The slot operators are cached, keyed on the carry and the step size,
so the probe runs only where the controller changed the control state.

Observations lie at interpolated times rather than at step ends, and are
evaluated through the continuous extension of the step that contains
them. The adjoint of that evaluation is obtained from the same probe:
after the tail has been applied the probe holds a valid interpolant, and
evaluating it at the observation time yields the row
$\partial x_{\text{interp}} / \partial (z^{\text{pred}}, a)$ directly.

### Checkpoint reuse

The sweep uses only the checkpoints, so the forward pass and the
backward pass can be issued as separate calls. A reverse solve with
\texttt{keepStore = TRUE} returns its checkpoints as \verb|$store|, and
a later solve of the same model at the same times and parameters accepts
them through \texttt{store}; that solve performs no integration and
proceeds directly to the sweep. A store created at a different parameter
value is rejected rather than reused. The cotangent may be omitted on
the call that creates a store, which then performs a value-only run and
retains its checkpoints.

A gradient requires two solves at the same parameter value, one to
provide the values from which the cotangent is formed and one to perform
the sweep, and the store removes the second integration. Several
cotangents are handled in the same way: the columns of a
three-dimensional cotangent sweep the one store in turn, so
$n_{\text{seed}}$ cotangents cost $n_{\text{seed}}$ sweeps and a single
integration.

Under \verb|derivMode = "forward-reverse"| both arguments are refused. A
checkpoint of that mode carries tangents, which live in the arena of the
solve that recorded them and do not outlive it, so every second-order
sweep is preceded by its own integration.

### The adjoint of an event

An event is a map of its own between two steps. The forward run
transports the discontinuity with the Heun sandwich of Section
\ref{sec:saltation}: a shift to the event surface, the resets, and a
shift back to the grid time. Each shift is taken over the residual of
the event time, which is zero in value and carries only derivatives.
In value the jump is therefore a plain jump, and the sandwich reduces
to the classical saltation relation,
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d}x = R'\!\left(\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s\right)
              - f_{\text{after}}\, s,
  \label{eq:saltation}
\end{equation}
with $R$ the resets, $R'$ their Jacobian and $s$ the differential of the
event time. For a root event $g(x, t, p) = 0$ the implicit function
theorem gives
$s = -(\nabla g \cdot \mathrm{d}x + \partial g/\partial p \cdot
\mathrm{d}p) / \dot g$, and for a fixed event at $t = \tau(p)$ it is
$s = (\partial \tau/\partial p)\cdot \mathrm{d}p$.

Since \eqref{eq:saltation} is linear in $\mathrm{d}x_{\text{before}}$
and $\mathrm{d}p$, its transpose can be read off directly. Contracting
it with a cotangent $\lambda_{\text{after}}$ and collecting the terms
that multiply $s$ leaves one scalar,
\begin{equation}
  \kappa = \lambda_{\text{after}}^{\mathsf T}
           \left(R' f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}}\right),
  \qquad
  \lambda_{\text{before}}
    = R'^{\mathsf T}\lambda_{\text{after}}
    + \kappa \left(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T},
  \label{eq:saltation-adjoint}
\end{equation}
and the parameter cotangent receives
$\kappa\,(\partial s/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}$ in addition. For a root
event both derivatives of $s$ carry the factor $-\kappa/\dot g$, so the
state picks up $-(\kappa/\dot g)\nabla g$ and the parameters
$-(\kappa/\dot g)\,\partial g/\partial p$. For a fixed event
$\partial s/\partial x = 0$ and the parameters pick up
$\kappa\,\partial\tau/\partial p$.

The transpose $R'^{\mathsf T}$ is applied reset by reset and in reverse
order. A reset that replaces a state removes the incoming cotangent of
that component, one that adds to it leaves the cotangent unchanged, and
one that multiplies it by $h$ scales it by $h$; where the reset value
$h$ depends on the state or on the parameters, its derivatives enter the
same transpose. The adjoint of a jump therefore requires the right-hand
side at the two ends, $\nabla g$ and $\dot g$, and the model's
derivatives of the reset and event-time expressions. It requires no
Jacobian of $f$, because every term the two shifts would contribute
carries the residual as a factor and that factor is zero.

After a jump the multistepper restarts. \verb|initialize| builds the
Nordsieck history from a single state as $z_0 = x$ and
$z_1 = h\, f(x, t)$, with the remaining slots zero, so the cotangent of
the history collapses onto that one state. Writing $w_j$ for the
cotangent of slot $j$, the restart contributes
\begin{equation}
  \bar x = w_0 + h\, J^{\mathsf T} w_1,
  \qquad
  \bar p = h \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T} w_1,
  \label{eq:restart-collapse}
\end{equation}
and slots above the first contribute nothing. The same map applies at
the start of the trajectory.

### Second order of an event's adjoint

Write $s$ for the differential of the event time, so that $s = 0$ in value and
$\mathrm{d}s \neq 0$. Then
\begin{equation}
  s^{2} = 0, \qquad \mathrm{d}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2 s\,\mathrm{d}s = 0,
  \qquad \mathrm{d}^{2}\!\left(s^{2}\right) = 2\,(\mathrm{d}s)^{2} \neq 0 ,
  \label{eq:s-squared}
\end{equation}
so terms of order $s^{2}$ drop from the gradient and not from the Hessian.
Three of them enter a jump. The same three enter a fixed event, with the event
time's own residual $\tau = \varepsilon(\theta) - \lfloor \varepsilon \rceil$ in
place of $s$: a fixed event is the same five-stage sandwich
\eqref{eq:root-sandwich}, and its transpose is that program reversed with $\tau$
substituted throughout. The classical saltation alone is exact in value and
wrong in the tangents as soon as the jump height moves with a parameter,
because $\bar x_{a} = (I - \tau J_{a})^{\mathsf T}\bar x_{o}$ then has a
second factor that is not zero in value.

The first term is the curvature of the shift. Each half of the sandwich is a
Heun step,
\begin{equation}
  x_{\ast} = x_{\text{before}} + f_{\text{before}}\, s
           + \tfrac{1}{2}\, a_{\text{before}}\, s^{2},
  \qquad
  a = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} f + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t},
  \label{eq:heun-curvature}
\end{equation}
and $a\,s$ is the difference of the two right-hand sides the step already
evaluates, so no Jacobian is needed.

The second is the post-jump state, which the sweep reconstructs, since the
store keeps $x_{\text{before}}$ alone. Rebuilt from the bare reset, it would
satisfy $\partial x_{\text{after}} / \partial t^{*} = 0$, whereas
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial x_{\text{after}}}{\partial t^{*}}
    = f_{\text{before}} - f_{\text{after}} .
  \label{eq:post-jump-motion}
\end{equation}
The reconstruction therefore runs the sandwich, not the reset.

The third comes from the quadrature. The parameter cotangent
\begin{equation}
  \bar p_{k} = \int_{0}^{T} G_{k}\,\mathrm{d}t
             = \int_{0}^{t^{*}} + \int_{t^{*}}^{T},
  \qquad
  G_{k} = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_{k}}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \label{eq:quadrature-split}
\end{equation}
is split at $t^{*}$, and $G_{k}$ is discontinuous there because the state is.
Differentiating a split integral whose split point moves leaves the jump of the
integrand at the split,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial \bar p_{k}}{\partial v}
  \;\supset\;
  \Big( G_{k}(t^{*-}) - G_{k}(t^{*+}) \Big)\,
  \frac{\partial t^{*}}{\partial v} .
  \label{eq:quadrature-jump}
\end{equation}
Only parameters whose $\partial f / \partial p_{k}$ depends on a state the reset
changed contribute.

Implemented as accumulations scaled by the residual, all three are zero in value
and carry $\partial t^{*} / \partial v$ in their tangent, so the gradient is
unchanged.

For a fixed event at $t = \tau(p)$ the residual is $\tau - \lfloor \tau \rceil$.
For a root event it is
\begin{equation}
  s = -\,\frac{g - \lfloor g \rceil}{\dot g},
  \qquad
  \dot g = \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} + \nabla g \cdot f ,
  \label{eq:root-residual}
\end{equation}
read at the stored state. Localisation ignores the tangents, so that state carries
$\partial x / \partial \theta$ at a fixed time and $\nabla g$ contracts it to
the event time's.

### Transposing the root sandwich

The jump is the composition
\begin{equation}
  x_{e} = x_{b} + f_{b} s, \quad
  x_{\ast} = x_{b} + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{b} + f_{e}) s, \quad
  x_{a} = R(x_{\ast}), \quad
  x_{k} = x_{a} - f_{a} s, \quad
  x_{o} = x_{a} - \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{a} + f_{k}) s ,
  \label{eq:root-sandwich}
\end{equation}
with $f_{e} = f(x_{e}, t^{*})$, $f_{a} = f(x_{a}, t^{*})$ and
$f_{k} = f(x_{k}, t_{0})$. Equation \eqref{eq:root-sandwich} is a straight-line
program, and its adjoint is obtained by reversing it assignment by assignment
rather than by collecting a closed form. A collected form pruned by order in
$s$, keeping a product only where one factor does not vanish in value, is
valid for the gradient and invalid for the Hessian: by \eqref{eq:s-squared},
$s^{2}$ has vanishing value and vanishing first derivative, while
$\mathrm{d}^{2}(s^{2}) = 2(\mathrm{d}s)^{2} \neq 0$.

Reversed assignment by assignment, the shift receives a contribution from every
assignment in which it occurs. Two of these arise because $f_{e}$ and $f_{a}$
are evaluated at $t^{*}$, which depends on $\theta$:
\begin{equation}
  \bar s \;\supset\;
    \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{a}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{a}
    + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}\right)_{\!(x_{e}, t^{*})}\!\!\cdot \bar f_{e} .
  \label{eq:shift-clock}
\end{equation}
Both cotangents carry a factor $s$, so \eqref{eq:shift-clock} is absent from the
gradient and contributes at full strength to the Hessian. It vanishes
identically for an autonomous right-hand side, and a pruned form omits it
whenever $\partial f/\partial t \neq 0$.

The forward path corrects the shift by $-\tfrac{1}{2}(\ddot g / \dot g)\,s^{2}$,
whose chain factor $1 + 2 c_{2} s$, $c_{2} = -\ddot g / (2\dot g)$, is one in
value and a second-order tangent; the transpose carries it on
$\partial s / \partial x$.

The implementation is checked in three ways. With $R = \mathrm{id}$ the composition
\eqref{eq:root-sandwich} is the identity and the transpose cancels term by term.
The transpose is compared with a nested-dual evaluation of the same sandwich,
without a solver, a store or an event engine. And a whole trajectory is compared
with forward over forward on one recorded step sequence. Only the third is
sensitive to \eqref{eq:shift-clock}: the second is checked against the same
forward routine the transpose reverses, so a term absent from both sides cancels.

The shift has a derivative of its own. Since $\dot g$ reads the state,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial s}{\partial x}
    = -\frac{\nabla g}{\dot g} - \frac{s}{\dot g}\, \nabla \dot g ,
  \qquad
  \nabla \dot g = \nabla \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}
                + \left(\nabla^{2} g\right) f + J^{\mathsf T}\nabla g ,
  \label{eq:root-quotient}
\end{equation}
and the second term carries $g$, which is zero in value: absent from the
gradient and full strength in the Hessian. For a $g$ that is linear in the state
and does not depend on time, $\nabla \dot g$ is $J^{\mathsf T}\nabla g$ alone,
so that case does not test the other two terms. The generator therefore differentiates
$\dot g = \partial g/\partial t + \nabla g \cdot f$ as one expression rather than
assembling three terms, which gives $\nabla \partial g/\partial t$ and
$(\nabla^{2} g) f$ with it, and on $\theta$ the matching
$\partial^{2} g/\partial\theta\,\partial t$,
$(\partial \nabla g/\partial\theta)\cdot f$ and
$(\partial f/\partial\theta)^{\mathsf T}\nabla g$. A forcing inside $g$ is
differentiated in $t$ through its rate: the time derivative on the expression
graph seeds each forcing leaf with a rate leaf, which prints as the derivative of
the PCHIP interpolant.

\textbf{Time-dependent resets.} A reset value $h$ that depends explicitly on
time is applied on the surface, at $t^{*}$, so
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial x_{a}}{\partial t^{*}} \;\supset\; c\,
  \frac{\partial h}{\partial t}, \qquad
  c = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{add} \\ 1 & \text{replace} \\ x_{\ast k} &
  \text{multiply,}\end{cases}
  \label{eq:reset-clock}
\end{equation}
which contributes to $\kappa$, the scalar multiplying the shift. This is a
first-order term: omitting it makes the gradient wrong, not only the Hessian.
For the same reason the transposed reset receives the event time as a dual
rather than as a plain number, so that $\partial h/\partial\theta$ carries the
dependence of $t^{*}$ on $\theta$.

Such a value inherits the root tolerance rather than the integration tolerance,
since it evaluates $t^{*}$ directly, whereas in a value that depends only on
the state at $t^{*}$ the localisation error is damped by the smoothness of the
trajectory.

Against the sandwich itself, evaluated over a nested dual with no solver around
it, the transpose is exact to $9\cdot10^{-16}$, and over a whole trajectory the
second order agrees with the forward mode to the tolerance of the solve.

Every buffer the sweep hands to a generated contraction has its tangent storage
bound by the sweep. The contraction opens an arena scope of its own, and an
output without bound storage would keep a tangent pointer into memory that scope
reclaims on exit. Since every read of such a buffer in the jump transpose is
multiplied by $s$, the value and the gradient would be unaffected, and the
Hessian would be wrong by a rank-one term.

### Verifying a derivative across a moving event

When $t^{*}$ depends on a parameter, the reported trajectory carries a row whose
time moves with it. A functional $w^{\mathsf T} x$ seeded on that row is not the
same functional at two parameter values and has no derivative to compare
against. Restricting the cotangent to the user's own output times restores a
well-posed functional, after which the forward, forward-over-forward and
difference-quotient answers agree to the tolerance of the solve.

### Internal numerical differentiation

The step sizes the controller selected are constants of the map that is
differentiated. This is Bock's internal numerical differentiation: the
nominal run adapts freely, and the derivative is taken of the scheme
that run applied. Differentiating the control law instead introduces
derivatives of the step sizes into the chain rule, which makes the
discrete adjoint inconsistent with the adjoint ODE. That term, measured
at $O(\text{tol})$, is left out.

This choice is often justified by the claim that $h$ is piecewise constant
in $\theta$, with zero derivative almost everywhere. An adaptive controller
does not produce such an $h$, and the argument below does not rely on it.

Let $y_{h}(\theta)$ denote the result the program returns on the grid the
controller selects at $\theta$. Then
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d} y_{h}}{\mathrm{d}\theta}
    = \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial \theta}
    + \sum_{k} \frac{\partial y_{h}}{\partial h_{k}}\,
      \frac{\mathrm{d} h_{k}}{\mathrm{d}\theta} ,
  \label{eq:grid-effect}
\end{equation}
where the first term is what internal numerical differentiation computes and
the sum is the grid effect, which differentiating the control law would add.

The function $h(\theta)$ is piecewise smooth with jumps. Within an acceptance
region it varies smoothly through the error estimate; at the boundary of one a
step that was accepted is rejected and the entire later grid shifts. Halving
the spacing of a sweep in $\theta$ doubles the measured magnitude of the grid
effect, which identifies it as a jump height divided by $\Delta\theta$ rather
than as a derivative. Automatic differentiation reproduces only the smooth part.
Differentiating the control law therefore returns the exact gradient plus the
smooth part of the grid effect, with the jump part, which is the larger of the
two, absent. The result is neither the derivative of the exact solution, to
which the addition does not belong, nor the derivative of the reported value,
of which the dominant contribution is missing. Recovering the grid effect
requires a smoothed controller, a fixed grid or a randomised estimator, none of
which differentiation of the existing chain provides.

By the same criterion it is the forward mode that departs from internal
numerical differentiation, not the reverse one. The value pass of the reverse
mode runs the stepper on plain numbers, so the step sizes follow from the
state error alone and the derivative is taken on the grid of the nominal run.
The forward mode with the default \texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} maximises its
error norm over the sensitivity columns as in \eqref{eq:wrms-sens} and
therefore integrates on a finer grid, to which no reported value belongs. The
reverse gradient is the derivative of the trajectory a value run returns, the
forward gradient the derivative of a trajectory that is not reported, and the
$O(\mathrm{tol})$ difference between them is mainly due to the forward mode.

The forward mode keeps the sensitivities in its error norm by default: they are
integrated alongside the state and their errors accumulate, which CVODES guards
against in the same way (\texttt{CVodeSetSensErrCon}). Value and gradient on
slightly different grids is the smaller cost.
\texttt{solveODE(..., sensErrCon = FALSE)} selects the alternative.

### Goal-oriented step-size control

A grid selected from the state error alone need not be fine enough for
the gradient. Since $\lambda$ is solved backwards, a step at which
$\lambda$ is large contributes strongly to the error in $J$ even where
its own state error is small; the gradient inherits the order of the
state error but not its constant. In the forward mode this is settled
within the run, by maximising the error norm over the sensitivity
columns as in \eqref{eq:wrms-sens}. In the reverse mode it cannot be,
because $\lambda$ at step $k$ depends on every step after it and is not
available while step $k$ is being taken.

It is available across runs. The \texttt{errWeights} argument of
\texttt{solveODE()} takes the $\lambda$ left by an earlier sweep,
sampled on that sweep's grid, reads it back by linear interpolation and
enters it into the error norm as
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{err} = \max\!\left(
    \mathrm{err}_{\text{state}},\;
    \frac{\left|\lambda(t_{n+1})^{\mathsf T} e_n\right|}{\mathtt{gradtol}}
  \right),
  \label{eq:goal-oriented}
\end{equation}
where $e_n$ is the embedded error estimate of the step. The numerator
estimates the contribution of this step to the error in the objective,
and \texttt{gradtol} is the tolerance to which that contribution is held,
which makes the two terms comparable.

Because of the maximum, the grid can only become finer than
\texttt{abstol} and \texttt{reltol} require, never coarser, so the
accuracy of the trajectory is unaffected. An inaccurate $\lambda$ costs
at most computing time: if it is too large the steps are unnecessarily
small, and if it is too small the state term governs as before. An
estimate of $\lambda$ from a neighbouring parameter value is therefore
admissible, so an optimiser can pass the sweep of iteration $i-1$ to
iteration $i$ and pay for one pass rather than two.

The weight is an input to the controller and is held in plain
\texttt{double}. The controller is not differentiated, and a weight
carried into the derivative would reintroduce the step-size term
discussed above. The interpolation is linear rather than PCHIP for the
same reason and for two further ones: $\lambda$ jumps where the
objective seeds it and where an event resets the state, so
\texttt{breaks} names the sample indices an interpolant must not span,
and a query inside such an interval takes the nearer endpoint; and shape
preservation is of no value for a weight whose overshoots cost only
time. A \texttt{floor} raises weights that fall below a given fraction
of the largest, which is a precaution rather than a necessity, since
$\lambda$ measures a linearised influence and a state it weights near
zero may still move nonlinearly.

The indicator can be inspected directly. With
\texttt{adjointGrid = TRUE} a reverse solve also returns the grid the
sweep ran on, $\lambda$ at the start of each step, and
$\eta_n = \lambda(t_{n+1})^{\mathsf T} e_n$ for each step, which is the
numerator of \eqref{eq:goal-oriented} and estimates that step's
contribution to the error in $J$. The estimate is of first order, since
it evaluates $\lambda$ at the computed rather than the exact state, and
what the adaptation requires of it is the ranking of the steps rather
than the magnitude.

### Relation to the forward mode

Forward and reverse derivatives of the same model do not agree to
machine precision. With \texttt{sensErrCon = TRUE} a sensitivity run
maximises its error norm over the state and every tangent column and
takes a finer grid than a value run at equal tolerances. The two modes
therefore differentiate two different discretisations, each exactly,
and the difference falls with the tolerance.

The reverse gradient is the derivative of the trajectory a value run
produces, so the value and the gradient returned to the caller are
consistent. A trust-region method, which compares a predicted with an
achieved reduction, relies on this.

Of the four methods, the Rosenbrock adjoint is the most accurate: its
stages are direct solves, so its adjoint is the exact transpose of the
discrete step, whereas the adjoint of a corrector applies the implicit
function theorem to an iteration stopped at a finite tolerance.

The reverse mode supports all four time-stepping methods, time- and
root-triggered events, forcings, the batch entry point and the sparse
linear solver. The implementation resides in
\texttt{cppde\_adjoint\_step.hpp}, \texttt{cppde\_reverse\_step.hpp}
and \texttt{cppde\_reverse\_trajectory.hpp}.

### Second derivatives: forward over reverse \label{sec:fwdrev}

For a fixed cotangent, \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction} defines the
gradient map
\begin{equation}
  \bar\theta : \mathbb{R}^{M} \to \mathbb{R}^{M},
  \qquad \theta \mapsto \nabla_\theta J(\theta),
  \label{eq:gradient-map}
\end{equation}
whose Jacobian is the Hessian $\nabla^2_\theta J$. Nothing in the sweep
that evaluates \eqref{eq:gradient-map} depends on the scalar type, so
instantiating it on $\mathtt{dual}\langle\mathtt{double}, N\rangle$
rather than on \texttt{double} differentiates the sweep itself. Seeded
with the tangent $V \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N}$ it returns the pair
$(\nabla_\theta J,\; \nabla^2_\theta J\,V)$, both computed exactly
rather than by a difference quotient; for $V = I_M$ the second member is
the Hessian. This is selected
by \texttt{derivMode = "forward-reverse"} and reported as
\verb|curvature|, of shape $[n_x + n_p, N, n_{\text{seed}}]$, beside the
\verb|cotangent| and \verb|tangent| of the same run.

The tangents satisfy the second-order adjoint system. Write
$v = (v_0, v_p)$ for one direction in $\theta$, let $\sigma$ be the
directional sensitivity and $\mu$ the tangent of $\lambda$ along $v$.
Then $\sigma$ solves \eqref{eq:sensitivity-p} contracted with $v$,
\begin{equation}
  \dot\sigma = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\,\sigma
             + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\,v_p,
  \qquad \sigma(t_0) = v_0,
  \label{eq:soa-tangent}
\end{equation}
and differentiating \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} along $v$ gives $\mu$
backwards from $\mu(T^+) = 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \dot\mu_i = -\sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial x_i}\,\mu_k
            - \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
                \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
              + \sum_m \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial x_i\, \partial p_m}\,v_m
              \right),
  \label{eq:soa-adjoint}
\end{equation}
and with the jumps $\mu(t_o^-) = \mu(t_o^+) + \dot w_o$, where
