$\dot w_o$ is the derivative of the cotangent row $w_o$ along $v$. It is
zero for a cotangent that does not depend on $\theta$; a cotangent formed
from the solution, such as a weighted residual, supplies it through the
\texttt{curvature} argument, an array
$[n_{\mathrm{out}}, n_x, n_{\mathrm{seed}}, N]$. Without it the gradient
is unchanged and the Hessian misses the dependence of the cotangent on
$\theta$. Differentiating
\eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature} along $v$ then gives the two halves of
$\nabla^2_\theta J\,v$, the state half as $\mu(t_0)$ and the parameter
half as
\begin{equation}
  \int_{t_0}^{T}\left(
      \sum_k \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial p_m}\,\mu_k
    + \sum_k \lambda_k \left(
        \sum_j \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial x_j}\,\sigma_j
      + \sum_l \frac{\partial^2 f_k}{\partial p_m\, \partial p_l}\,v_l
      \right)\right)\mathrm{d}t .
  \label{eq:soa-quadrature}
\end{equation}
cppDE does not integrate \eqref{eq:soa-tangent} to
\eqref{eq:soa-quadrature}. It obtains their discrete counterpart from
the dual instantiation: the tangent carried alongside $\lambda$ is $\mu$
on the grid the forward run chose, and the tangent of the parameter
accumulator is \eqref{eq:soa-quadrature}. The second derivatives of $f$
that appear in \eqref{eq:soa-adjoint} and \eqref{eq:soa-quadrature} are
supplied by instantiating the first-order contractions
$J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ and $(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$
over duals, so forward over reverse needs no generated expression beyond
those of the first-order sweep. For a Rosenbrock method these already
include the contractions of $J v$, which are second derivatives of $f$.

The tangents have to be present in the forward pass as well, since the
sweep reads its checkpoints, which makes that pass a sensitivity run in
the same $N$ directions. Its error control reads the values only, so it
takes the grid of a value run. The cost is one sensitivity integration and one
sweep, both of width $N$, and therefore linear in $N$. Forward over
forward, selected by \texttt{derivMode = "forward-forward"} or by the
older \texttt{deriv2 = TRUE}, propagates the full second-order
sensitivity tensor through the integration at a cost quadratic in $M$. A
difference quotient of the gradient would cost $N$ further gradient
evaluations and lose half of the available digits.

Forward over forward answers a different question. It returns
\verb|hessian|, the second derivatives of every state
with respect to every pair of parameters, from which the Hessian of any
functional can be contracted afterwards. Forward over reverse returns
the Hessian of one functional. Where that functional is a likelihood the
mixed route is the cheaper by a factor of $M$; where the states
themselves are of interest, only \verb|hessian| answers.

The second order needs two further facilities. The iteration matrix
carries tangents, so the transposed solve applies the implicit function
theorem with the matrix transposed alongside;
\texttt{cppde\_ad\_lu.hpp} and \texttt{cppde\_sparse\_ad\_lu.hpp}
provide this in the dense and the sparse case. And a generated model
body opens an arena scope of its own, in which a tangent allocated for
one of the caller's numbers would be released, so the sweep binds the
tangent storage of every buffer before passing it to the model, as the
stepper does for its own buffers through the tangent slab.

The two second-order routes agree to $10^{-6}$ on \texttt{bdf},
\texttt{rb4} and \texttt{tsit5}, and all four methods return the same
Hessian in reverse to $10^{-5}$. The second comparison is the stronger
one: the four methods adapt grids of their own, so agreement means that
each sweep differentiated the discretisation its own method applied.

## Batches of conditions \label{sec:batch}

\texttt{solveODEBatch()} solves $K$ conditions of one model in a single
\texttt{.Call}, in three phases. The first reads the arguments of every
condition from R into plain C++ structures, on the main thread. The
second runs the $K$ solves on OpenMP threads with dynamic scheduling, so
a slow condition does not hold up the others; the workers touch neither
the R API nor R's allocator, which is not thread-safe. The third builds
the result list, again on the main thread. When the output grid is fixed
by \texttt{times}, the result arrays are allocated before the second
phase and the workers write into them directly; a root event leaves the
row count open until the solve ends, and its output is copied afterwards.

Each condition is solved as \texttt{solveODE()} would solve it: the
workers share no state and form no reductions across conditions, so the
result is bitwise identical to the serial loop, whatever the thread
count and schedule.

The thread count is the smaller of the request and $K$. It falls to one
inside an enclosing OpenMP region, where the caller already runs in
parallel, and in a child created by \texttt{fork()}, because the OpenMP
thread pool does not survive a fork; a \texttt{pthread\_atfork} handler
marks the child. The BLAS library's own threads are set to one for the
duration of a batch and restored afterwards, and the same handler does
so around every \texttt{fork()}. \texttt{forkGuard()} reports which BLAS
library was found, and \texttt{batchAvailable()} whether a model runs
its conditions in parallel.

\texttt{prepareBatch()} performs the first phase once and keeps the
converted arguments in a handle. \texttt{solveBatch()} then solves the
same conditions with new parameter values, tangents, cotangents
or error weights of unchanged shapes, as an optimiser does at every
iteration. Reverse-mode solves run through the same entry with one
cotangent per condition, and \texttt{cvode()} models provide the same batch
entry.

# \texttt{cvode()} \label{sec:cvode}

The \texttt{cvode()} entry point compiles a model against the
system-installed SUNDIALS CVODE/CVODES library and exposes the
result through the same \texttt{solveODE()} interface as
\texttt{cppODE()}. The code generator, the \texttt{events},
\texttt{forcings}, \texttt{rootfunc} and \texttt{fixed} arguments, the
shape of the returned object, and the column ordering of
\texttt{parms} and \texttt{tangent} are the same for both backends.
SUNDIALS ($\ge 6.0$) must be installed on the build host; KLU, used for
sparse Jacobians, is detected the same way and is required when
\texttt{sparse = TRUE}.

## What is shared

The Jacobian $J = \partial f / \partial x$ is formed on the expression
graph of Section \ref{sec:codegen} and emitted as C++ as in
\texttt{cppODE()}, including its linear tables and loops. Both backends
select the sparse KLU solver automatically for $n_x \ge 8$ states and a
structural density of $J$ of at most $0.4$, provided SuiteSparse was
found at install time, and dense LAPACK otherwise. Forcing functions
are PCHIP interpolants, events apply a discontinuous reset to the
state, and root events fire when a user-supplied scalar function
crosses zero.

## What differs

\textbf{Sensitivity right-hand side.} CVODES integrates the
forward-sensitivity equation
\begin{equation}
  \dot S_k = J(x, p)\, S_k + \frac{\partial f}{\partial p_k},
  \qquad k = 1, \dots, n_p,
  \label{eq:cvodes-sens}
\end{equation}
directly. The generated right-hand side of \eqref{eq:cvodes-sens} is
one Jacobian-vector product of $f$ in the direction
$(S_k, \partial p/\partial\theta_k)$, evaluated in \texttt{double}
without forming $J$. The in-tree backend recovers the same equation by
evaluating $f$ on dual-typed state, cf.\ \eqref{eq:sensitivity-p}.
The two formulations are mathematically equivalent. Numerically, the
generated product avoids the per-evaluation arena allocation required
by the dual-number path, but is invoked once per direction, whereas
the dual evaluation carries all directions in a single pass.

\textbf{Methods.} CVODE provides only the multistep families,
selected by \texttt{cvode(method = "bdf")} or
\texttt{cvode(method = "adams")}; \texttt{rb4} and \texttt{tsit5} are
not available. The stability properties of Section \ref{sec:cppde}
apply unchanged.

\textbf{Second-order sensitivities.} CVODES provides only first-order
forward sensitivities, and \texttt{cvode()} does not accept
\texttt{deriv2 = TRUE}.

\textbf{Events.} Events on \texttt{cvode()} models use the Heun
transport of \texttt{cppODE()}, with the first-order corrections
\eqref{eq:fixed-heun} and \eqref{eq:dt-star-first}. The transport runs
in the generated glue rather than inside CVODES, which re-initialises
its sensitivities from the transported state.

\textbf{Seeding.} The chain-rule construction
$S_\theta = S_p\,\partial p / \partial \theta$ of equation
\eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta} is identical to the \texttt{cppODE()}
case. \texttt{solveODE()} accepts the same \texttt{tangent} matrix
shapes (state-only, full, and partial) and the same row-name conventions;
only second-order $S_\theta$ is unavailable.

## Adjoint sensitivity analysis \label{sec:asa}

\texttt{cvode(..., derivMode = "reverse")} compiles the CVODES adjoint
sensitivity analysis (ASA) in place of the forward sensitivities and
returns the same \verb|$cotangent| as a native reverse solve, the
contraction \eqref{eq:adjoint-contraction} of a cotangent, stacked states
first and parameters second. The rest of the call, including the batch
entry point, is unchanged.

\textbf{Backward problem.} Where \texttt{cppODE()} transposes the
steps the forward run took, CVODES integrates \eqref{eq:adjoint-ode} as
an ODE in its own right [@cao2003adjoint]. The generated glue emits the
two transposed contractions as vector-Jacobian products of $f$
(Section \ref{sec:codegen}),
\begin{equation}
  \dot\lambda = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \qquad
  \dot q = -\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}\right)^{\!\mathsf T}\!\lambda,
  \label{eq:asa-system}
\end{equation}
the second of which is the quadrature of
\eqref{eq:adjoint-quadrature} with $q(T) = 0$. CVODES carries it
alongside the backward state and leaves it out of the error test, its
default: with gradient entries of very different scale the test would
stall the backward step. Both equations are
integrated from $T$ down to $t_0$, and the minus signs of
\eqref{eq:asa-system} cancel against the reversed limits, so $q(t_0)$
is the parameter part of the gradient and $\lambda(t_0)$ the state
part. Both right-hand sides are the contractions the native reverse
mode uses; neither forms $J$.

\textbf{Checkpoints.} The backward right-hand side needs $x(t)$, which
the forward pass no longer holds. CVODES stores a checkpoint every
\texttt{asaCheckpoints} accepted steps, $200$ by default, and recovers
the states between two checkpoints by re-integrating forward from the
earlier one and interpolating; the argument trades memory against that
re-integration. This is the main difference between the two
discretisations: the adjoint sees interpolated states rather than the
ones the forward run stepped through, so the gradient is the
derivative of no discretisation that was carried out. It approximates
the exact gradient to $O(\mathrm{tol})$ and differs by the same order
from the derivative of the value the call reported.

\textbf{Jumps at observations.} $\lambda$ is initialised with the cotangent
row of the last observation, and the sweep stops at every earlier
observation time to add that row, the jump condition in
\eqref{eq:adjoint-ode}. A jump is a new initial condition, so the
backward problem is re-initialised wherever a row is nonzero, and only
there: re-initialising at every output time would reduce the method to
first order at times the objective does not observe. The backward
problem is a BDF solve with the linear solver of the forward problem,
KLU for a sparse model, and the analytic Jacobian $-J^{\top}$, formed
from $J$ in the forward pattern; it runs at the caller's tolerances and
step budget.

\textbf{Several cotangents.} The columns of a cotangent share the checkpoints,
but each needs a backward integration of its own. The native mode
sweeps its stored checkpoints once per column instead. Its
\texttt{keepStore}, \texttt{store}, \texttt{adjointGrid} and
\texttt{errWeights} arguments have no counterpart here, since CVODES
holds its own checkpoints and runs its own backward controller.

\textbf{Restrictions.} Events and root functions are rejected at
code-generation time, since a jump in the state implies a jump in
$\lambda$ and ASA has no interface to apply one. Forward sensitivities
cannot be requested for the same model, and there is no second-order
mode. An event model, a Hessian, or a gradient consistent with the
value it accompanies therefore requires the native backend.

ASA is an independent implementation of the same mathematics and
serves as a check on the in-tree adjoint: the two agree to $10^{-6}$
on the test models.

# \texttt{cppFUN()} \label{sec:funcpp}

\texttt{cppFUN()} compiles a system of algebraic expressions
\begin{equation}
  y_i = g_i(x_1, \dots, x_{n_x}, p_1, \dots, p_{n_p}),
  \qquad i = 1, \dots, n_y,
  \label{eq:funcpp}
\end{equation}
with its first and second derivatives. The variables $x$ are supplied
per observation, as the rows of an $n_{\mathrm{obs}} \times n_x$ matrix,
and the parameters $p$ are shared by all rows. There is no time
integration. Typical uses are observation maps, which connect
integrator output to data and whose derivatives enter the gradient of a
likelihood, and reparametrisations $p = \Phi(\theta)$, whose Jacobian is
the tangent of \eqref{eq:sensitivity-theta}.

The expressions are parsed into the expression graph of Section
\ref{sec:codegen}, and the generator emits one function template over
the scalar type that evaluates $g$ for one observation. It is
instantiated on \texttt{double}, on \texttt{cppde::dual<double, 0>} and
on the nested dual \texttt{cppde::dual2nd<double, 0>}. The
vector-Jacobian product is a reverse sweep on the same graph, emitted as
a second template and instantiated on \texttt{double} and on the dual.

Every entry runs compiled code. With the default \texttt{compile = FALSE}
the constructor only writes the source, and the returned object has to
be passed to \texttt{compile()} before use; calling a function of an
uncompiled object stops with an error.

## Entry points and derivative directions

The argument \texttt{derivMode} names the derivative directions that are
built, \verb|"forward"|, \verb|"reverse"| or both, which is the default;
naming one direction omits the entries of the other, and their compile
time. \texttt{deriv} and \texttt{deriv2} switch the first- and
second-order entries, and \texttt{deriv2 = TRUE} requires
\verb|"forward"|. Table \ref{tab:funcpp-dispatch} lists the R functions
of the returned object and the compiled entries they call.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l @{}}
\toprule
R function & direction & compiled entry \\
\midrule
\texttt{func(x, p)}                                            & both    & \texttt{\_eval\_c} \\
\texttt{jac(x, p[, tangentX, tangentP])}                       & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_c} \\
\texttt{hess(x, p[, tangentX, tangentP, hessianX, hessianP])}  & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_c} \\
\texttt{evaluate(\ldots, deriv2)}                              & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_c} or \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_c} \\
\texttt{evaluateBatch(sets, cores, deriv2)}                    & forward & \texttt{\_eval\_ad\_batch} or \texttt{\_eval\_ad2\_batch} \\
\texttt{vjp(x, p, cotangent)}                                  & reverse & \texttt{\_vjp\_c} \\
\texttt{vjp(x, p, cotangent, tangentX, tangentP, curvature)}   & reverse & \texttt{\_vjp\_ad\_c} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{R functions of a \texttt{cppFUN()} object and the compiled
entries they call, each prefixed by the model name. The \texttt{\_c}
entries are \texttt{.Call} interfaces that take their arguments by
reference; \texttt{\_eval}, \texttt{\_eval\_ad}, \texttt{\_eval\_ad2} and
\texttt{\_vjp} also exist as \texttt{.C} interfaces, used only for a
shared object without the \texttt{.Call} symbol.}
\label{tab:funcpp-dispatch}
\end{table}

\textbf{Forward direction.} \texttt{jac} evaluates $g$ on duals and
returns $\partial y/\partial\theta$ as an array
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_\theta]$, \texttt{hess} evaluates it on
nested duals and returns $\partial^2 y/\partial\theta^2$ as
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_\theta, n_\theta]$. The directions $\theta$
are given by the tangents of the next section. Without them, the identity
over the variables and the differentiated parameters is used, so the
result is the Jacobian or Hessian with respect to $(x, p)$.
\texttt{evaluate} returns the value and the derivatives of one pass,
which separate calls of \texttt{func}, \texttt{jac} and \texttt{hess}
would evaluate up to three times, as \texttt{y}, \texttt{tangent} and,
with \texttt{deriv2 = TRUE}, \texttt{hessian}. \texttt{evaluateBatch} runs
\texttt{evaluate} over a list of argument sets in one call, distributed
over OpenMP threads with dynamic scheduling, and falls back to a loop
for fewer than two sets.

\textbf{Reverse direction.} For a cotangent $w$ of the outputs,
$[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y]$ or $[n_{\mathrm{obs}}, n_y, n_{\mathrm{seed}}]$,
\texttt{vjp} returns
\begin{equation}
  (w_x)_{o j s} = \sum_{i} w_{o i s}\,
      \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j}(x_o, p),
  \qquad
  (w_p)_{k s} = \sum_{o} \sum_{i} w_{o i s}\,
      \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial p_k}(x_o, p),
  \label{eq:funcpp-vjp}
\end{equation}
as \texttt{cotangentX} and \texttt{cotangentP}, together with the value
$y$. The parameter cotangent is summed over the
observations because the parameters are shared by them. The contraction
is one reverse sweep per observation and cotangent column, at a cost
independent of the number of upstream parameters, and forms neither the
Jacobian nor the Hessian. Statements of the sweep that do not depend on
the cotangent are evaluated once per observation, outside the loop over
cotangent columns.

Given \texttt{tangentX} and \texttt{tangentP}, the tangents $v_x$ and
$v_p$ of the inputs in $n_{\mathrm{dir}}$ directions, or
\texttt{curvature}, the derivative $\dot w$ of the cotangent along them,
\texttt{vjp} runs the same template on duals and returns, beside
\texttt{cotangentX} and \texttt{cotangentP}, the derivatives
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}v}\bigl(w^{\mathsf T} J\bigr)
    = w^{\mathsf T}\,\frac{\partial J}{\partial (x, p)}\,v
      + \dot w^{\mathsf T} J,
  \qquad J = \frac{\partial g}{\partial (x, p)},
  \label{eq:funcpp-vjp-curvature}
\end{equation}
as \texttt{curvatureX} and \texttt{curvatureP}. This is forward over
reverse as in Section \ref{sec:fwdrev}: an observation map contributes
its curvature to a backward chain without forming a Hessian.

## Tangent, Hessian, cotangent and curvature

A map has a tangent and a Hessian, a functional has a cotangent and a
curvature. For the upstream map $\Phi: \theta \mapsto (x, p)$ the
tangent is $V = \Phi'(\theta)$ and the Hessian is $\Phi''(\theta)$. For
a scalar functional of the outputs the cotangent $W$ is its gradient in
the outputs, and the curvature $\dot W$ is the derivative of $W$ along
the tangent, which is the Hessian of the functional applied to the
tangent. An argument and its result carry the same name: a forward
argument lives on the inputs and its result on the outputs, a reverse
argument lives on the outputs and its result on the inputs.
Table \ref{tab:derivative-names} lists the names.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{} l l l l @{}}
\toprule
object & \texttt{solveODE()} & \texttt{cppFUN()} argument & \texttt{cppFUN()} result \\
\midrule
tangent $V$        & \texttt{tangent}   & \texttt{tangentX}, \texttt{tangentP} & \texttt{tangent} \\
Hessian $\Phi''$   & \texttt{hessian}   & \texttt{hessianX}, \texttt{hessianP} & \texttt{hessian} \\
cotangent $W$      & \texttt{cotangent} & \texttt{cotangent}                   & \texttt{cotangentX}, \texttt{cotangentP} \\
curvature $\dot W$ & \texttt{curvature} & \texttt{curvature}                   & \texttt{curvatureX}, \texttt{curvatureP} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Names of the four derivative objects in R. \texttt{solveODE()}
uses one name for the argument and the element of its result; the
\texttt{cppFUN()} results are elements of the lists that
\texttt{evaluate} and \texttt{vjp} return.}
\label{tab:derivative-names}
\end{table}

Forward over forward takes $\Phi''$ as \texttt{hessian} and returns
\texttt{hessian}, the second derivatives of every output in every pair of
directions of the tangent. Forward over reverse takes $\dot W$ as
\texttt{curvature} and returns \texttt{curvature}, the Hessian of the
seeded functional applied to the tangent; with the identity tangent,
the columns of that Hessian.

\textbf{Chain rule.} \texttt{cppFUN()} takes the tangent and the Hessian
of its inputs in two blocks each:
\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{tangentX[obs, name, theta]}: $\partial x_i/\partial\theta_a$,
per observation row, variable and direction $\theta_a$;
\item \texttt{tangentP[name, theta]}: $\partial p_j/\partial\theta_a$, the
same for all observations;
\item \texttt{hessianX[obs, name, theta1, theta2]}:
$\partial^2 x_i/\partial\theta_a\partial\theta_b$, optional, zero by
default;
\item \texttt{hessianP[name, theta1, theta2]}:
$\partial^2 p_j/\partial\theta_a\partial\theta_b$, optional, zero by
default.
\end{itemize}
They may also be supplied as the attributes \texttt{deriv} and
\texttt{deriv2} of the variables and parameters. Tangent rows of
parameters listed in \texttt{fixed} are set to zero, and symbols absent
from the tangent contribute zero.

With the tangents bundled into one array
$V \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{obs}} \times n_{\mathrm{diff}} \times
n_\theta}$ over the $n_{\mathrm{diff}} = n_x + n_p$ inputs, and $\Phi''$
for the Hessians, the chain rule for the Jacobian reads
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta}\bigg|_{\mathrm{obs}}
    = J\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \cdot V_{\mathrm{obs}},
\end{equation}
and for the Hessian of output $o$ two contributions combine,
\begin{equation}
  \frac{\partial^2 y_o}{\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top}\bigg|_{\mathrm{obs}}
    = V_{\mathrm{obs}}^\top \, H_o\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \,
      V_{\mathrm{obs}}
    + \sum_{i} J_{o, i}\bigl(x_{\mathrm{obs}}, p\bigr) \,
        \Phi''_{\mathrm{obs}, i, \cdot, \cdot},
\end{equation}
the second of which vanishes when $\Phi$ is affine.

Neither $J$ nor $H$ is formed. Both contractions follow from seeding the
tangent slots of the duals. Each input scalar $x_i$ becomes
\begin{equation*}
  \tilde x_i = (x_i + V_{i,\cdot}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}})
             + \bigl(V_{i,\cdot}
                     + \Phi''_{i,\cdot,\cdot}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\bigr)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}},
\end{equation*}
a nested dual whose inner tangent slots carry $\partial x_i/\partial\theta$
and whose outer tangent slot $k$ is itself an inner dual with value
$\partial x_i/\partial\theta_k$ and inner tangents
$\partial^2 x_i/\partial\theta_k\partial\theta$. The multiplication rule
then propagates both the $V^\top H V$ and the $J \cdot \Phi''$ terms in one
evaluation; the inner tangents of $\tilde y$ are
$\partial y/\partial\theta$, and the cross slots $\tilde y[k][m]$ are
$\partial^2 y/\partial\theta_k\partial\theta_m$.

## Pass-through of unmodelled inputs

With \texttt{attach.input = TRUE}, inputs that do not appear among the
variables and parameters of \eqref{eq:funcpp} are appended to the output
unchanged: their values are copied, their Jacobian rows are zero for a
variable and the identity for a parameter, and their Hessian rows are
zero. An observation map then need not repeat every column of the
integrator output as an identity, as with the partial-shape
\texttt{tangent} of \texttt{solveODE()}.

\clearpage

# Benchmarks \label{sec:bench}

Both backends solve the same problem from the same model equations.
Right-hand side, analytic Jacobian, events, linear-solver selection,
and tolerances are shared, and both backends take their right-hand
side and Jacobian from the same expression graph, so a head-to-head
measurement isolates the numerical core rather than the model
formulation.

\textbf{Setup.} The suite comprises $43$ problems: $33$ published
systems-biology models from a PEtab benchmark collection and $10$
classical test problems (van der Pol at $\mu = 1000$, Robertson,
OREGO, HIRES, E5, Pollution, and method-of-lines semidiscretisations
of the one-dimensional Brusselator and FitzHugh-Nagumo systems at
$N = 24$ and $N = 64$). The state dimension ranges from $n_x = 2$ to
$504$. First-order sensitivities run forward for up to $M = 32$
differentiated parameters, the first $32$ where a model estimates more,
and in reverse from $M = 120$ on, which concerns
Lang\_PLOSComputBiol2024 ($n_x = 124$, $M = 164$) and Chen\_MSB2009
($n_x = 504$, $M = 152$). Both backends run their BDF/NDF method with
the automatically selected linear solver at
$(\mathrm{rtol}, \mathrm{atol}) \in \{(10^{-4}, 10^{-6}),
(10^{-7}, 10^{-9}), (10^{-10}, 10^{-12})\}$. Each cell repeats the
solve until one batch exceeds $0.25$ s and reports the median of five
such batches. The suite ran on two AMD EPYC 7513 nodes with twelve
workers each; both backends of a cell run in the same worker, so a
ratio compares like with like, while absolute times are comparable
within one node only. Figure \ref{fig:bench} shows the ratio
$r = t_{\texttt{cvode()}} / t_{\texttt{cppODE()}}$ per problem,
aggregated over the three tolerances by geometric mean.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-speedup.pdf}
\caption{Head-to-head ratio of the two backends, one marker per
problem and mode; above the line \texttt{cppODE()} is faster. The
abscissa is the number of parameters the model differentiates, which
the plain solve does not use. Its markers are placed at the same
abscissa as their sensitivity counterparts, and their flat course
shows that the $M$ dependence belongs to the sensitivity mode alone.}
\label{fig:bench}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Plain solves.} The in-tree backend is faster on all
$43$ problems, by a geometric mean of $1.17$, and the ratio is flat in
$M$. The two backends take the same steps: the geometric means of the
accepted-step and right-hand-side evaluation ratios are $1.02$ and
$1.06$, which rules out a margin bought by integrating more loosely.
The controller, the order selection, and the error constants of the
in-tree multistepper are those of CVODE, so the margin is a
cost-per-step effect. It arises from model specialisation: the
right-hand side and the Jacobian are emitted as straight-line C++ and
instantiated into the stepper as a functor template, so the calls
inline, whereas CVODES reaches them through a function pointer with a
\texttt{void*} user-data argument; the in-tree state vectors are
contiguous with the extent known at the call site, whereas every
SUNDIALS vector operation is dispatched through the operation table of
the \texttt{N\_Vector} it acts on.

\textbf{Forward sensitivities.} The in-tree backend is faster on
$33$ of $41$ problems, by a geometric mean of $1.28$, and
Figure \ref{fig:bench} shows that the ratio grows with $M$: $0.99$
over the nine problems with $M \le 3$, $1.22$ over the fourteen with
$4 \le M \le 12$, and $1.51$ over the eighteen with $13 \le M \le 32$.
CVODES is driven in staggered mode with an analytic sensitivity
right-hand side, one Jacobian-vector product per differentiated
parameter and corrector iteration. The in-tree backend obtains the same
$M$ columns from a single evaluation of $f$ on a dual-typed state that
carries all $M$ tangents, and reaches the same trajectories with about
one eleventh of the right-hand-side evaluations.

\textbf{Problems below parity.} The dual evaluation carries a
cost per state component that is independent of $M$: the arithmetic on
the value part, the tangent-slab bookkeeping, and the loss of the
vectorisation the scalar loop admits. The in-tree sensitivity work
therefore scales as $n_x\,(a + b\,M)$ with $a > 0$, whereas the CVODES
work scales as $M$ times the cost of one Jacobian-vector product. For a
method-of-lines discretisation that product costs
$\mathcal{O}(n_x)$, the state dimension cancels, and the comparison
reduces to $a + b\,M$ against $\mathcal{O}(M)$: small $M$ favours
CVODES, and the more so the larger $n_x$ is, since $a$ is paid per
component and amortised only over $M$. Six of the eight problems below
the parity line with sensitivities have $M \le 6$:
SalazarCavazos\_MBoC2020 ($n_x = 75$, $M = 6$) at $0.68$, van der Pol
($M = 1$) at $0.78$, the Brusselator at $N = 64$ and $N = 24$
($M = 3$) at $0.83$ and $0.88$, Perelson\_Science1996 ($M = 2$) at
$0.87$ and Bertozzi\_PNAS2020 ($M = 3$) at $0.95$. The remaining two,
Giordano\_Nature2020 and Oliveira\_NatCommun2021, lie within
$3\,\%$ of parity.

\textbf{Reverse sensitivities.} From $M = 120$ on the suite computes the
gradient of the sum of all outputs with the discrete adjoint of
Section \ref{sec:reverse}, one backward sweep over the recorded steps.
Figure \ref{fig:gradient} expresses every gradient in units of the
plain solve of the same problem. The forward cost is linear in $M$,
$1.9 + 0.60\,M$ for the in-tree backend and $1.1 + 0.85\,M$ for
CVODES, which extrapolates to about $93$ and $130$ plain solves at
$M = 152$. The adjoint costs $6.3$ plain solves for
Chen\_MSB2009 and $3.6$ for Lang\_PLOSComputBiol2024, independent of
$M$. Against a reference gradient at the reference tolerance, the
Chen gradient deviates by $4.9 \cdot 10^{-11}$ at
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-gradient.pdf}
\caption{Cost of one gradient in units of the plain solve of the same
problem, one marker per problem, geometric mean over the three
tolerances. The lines are least-squares fits of the forward cost,
linear in $M$, continued dashed beyond the measured range to the two
models that run in reverse.}
\label{fig:gradient}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Discrete and CVODES adjoint.} A separate run computes the same
gradient with both adjoints on the six models with $M \ge 40$, on one
node with one core per model. Two of them, Chen\_MSB2009 and
Giordano\_Nature2020, carry events, which the CVODES adjoint module does
not support. On the other four (Figure \ref{fig:adjoint}) the CVODES
adjoint takes $8.7$ to $18.8$ times as long as the discrete adjoint on
Lang\_PLOSComputBiol2024, Lucarelli\_CellSystems2018 and
Raimundez\_PCB2020, and $1.0$ to $1.5$ times on Zheng\_PNAS2012
($n_x = 15$), where a solve takes about a millisecond. The discrete
adjoint runs backward over the recorded steps of the forward solve;
CVODES integrates the backward problem with its own step-size control
and recomputes the forward state between checkpoints. At
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$ both gradients deviate from the reference by
$10^{-10}$ to $5 \cdot 10^{-7}$; the reference is the CVODES adjoint at
the reference tolerance, which favours CVODES. On Zheng\_PNAS2012 the
gradient of the summed outputs vanishes, so that model contributes a
timing only.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-adjoint.pdf}
\caption{Time of one gradient by the CVODES adjoint over the time by the
discrete adjoint, per model and tolerance; right of the line the
discrete adjoint is faster.}
\label{fig:adjoint}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Second order.} The Hessian of the sum of all outputs is
measured for the in-tree backend alone, on models with at most
$30$ states: forward over reverse (Section \ref{sec:fwdrev}) with up to
$32$ directions, and forward over forward, whose $M(M+1)/2$
second-order directions restrict it to models with at most $10$ states
and $10$ directions. Where both run they share the directions.
Figure \ref{fig:hessian} shows the cost in plain solves. Fitted in
log-log, forward over forward grows with an exponent of $1.9$, forward
over reverse with $0.6$. The two meet at $M \approx 3$: the ratio of
forward over forward to forward over reverse is $0.76$ at $M \le 2$,
$1.06$ at $M = 3$, $3.5$ at $M = 6$ and $7$, and $9.5$ at $M = 9$ and
$10$. At $\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$ the two Hessians deviate from the
forward-over-forward Hessian at the reference tolerance by a median of
$8.1 \cdot 10^{-10}$ and $1.8 \cdot 10^{-8}$.

\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig-hessian.pdf}
\caption{Cost of one Hessian of the summed outputs in units of the
plain solve, one marker per problem and mode, geometric mean over the
three tolerances. The lines are power laws fitted in log-log over
$M > 1$; their exponents are given in the legend.}
\label{fig:hessian}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!b]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.5\textwidth]{fig-sparse.pdf}
\caption{Gain of the sparse over the dense linear solver, one marker
per model and backend, geometric mean over tolerances and modes.}
\label{fig:sparse}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Linear solver and accuracy.} Seventeen of the models were
additionally solved with the linear solver pinned to dense and to
sparse. Figure \ref{fig:sparse} shows that the gain of the sparse path
grows with the state dimension in the same way for both backends, from
$1.08$ at $n_x = 8$ to about $3$ at $n_x \ge 128$, and the
auto-detection selected the sparse path, the faster one, in every
swept case, so Figure \ref{fig:bench} is a comparison at matched linear
algebra. Every solve was additionally scored against a reference
trajectory at $\mathrm{atol} = 10^{-14}$, $\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-12}$.
Per problem, the deviation of the in-tree backend is a median $1.01$
times that of CVODE without sensitivities, with the central $90\,\%$ of
the problems between $0.43$ and $1.52$, and $1.00$ with
sensitivities, between $0.49$ and $1.64$. The two are not on equal
footing there: the reference is itself a CVODE solution, so CVODE is
measured against a tighter run of the same method through the same
code, whose truncation error is structurally its own, while the
in-tree backend is measured across implementations. The bias runs in
CVODE's favour, which makes the quoted ratio an upper bound.

Fifteen of the $1083$ cells failed and are excluded from the
aggregates: the CVODES adjoint on Lang\_PLOSComputBiol2024 on each of
its three linear-solver settings and tolerances, which stalled at the
final time while its gradient quadrature was part of the error test and
completes in the configuration of Section \ref{sec:asa}, and at
$\mathrm{rtol} = 10^{-10}$ the in-tree forward sensitivities of
Oliveira\_NatCommun2021 on its three linear-solver settings and of
Weber\_BMC2015, as well as forward over forward on the same two
models.

# BDF and NDF coefficients

\label{app:bdf-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} [@MATLABODESuite], Table 1; cppDE
implementation in \texttt{cppde\_multistepper.hpp}.

The Numerical Differentiation Formula (NDF) of order $q$ modifies
the classical BDF$q$ corrector by adding a term proportional to
the Nordsieck predictor error,
\[
  \sum_{m=1}^{q} \frac{1}{m}\, \nabla^{m} x_n
  \;-\; h_n\, f(x_n, t_n)
  \;-\; \kappa_q\, \gamma_q\, \bigl(x_n - x_n^{\mathrm{pred}}\bigr)
  \;=\; 0,
  \qquad
  \gamma_q \;=\; \sum_{m=1}^{q} \tfrac{1}{m}.
\]
Setting $\kappa_q = 0$ recovers BDF$q$. The values $\kappa_q$
adopted by cppDE (selectable at compile time via the argument
\texttt{useNDF}, default \texttt{TRUE}) are tabulated in
Table \ref{tab:ndf-kappa}, together with the empirical step-size
gain over classical BDF$q$ and the resulting stability angle.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{} c S[table-format=-1.4] l l @{}}
\toprule
$q$ & {$\kappa_q$} & Step-size gain over BDF$q$ & Stability angle \\
\midrule
1 & -0.1850 & $+26\,\%$ & A-stable           \\
2 & -0.1111 & $+26\,\%$ & A-stable           \\
3 & -0.0823 & $+26\,\%$ & $80^\circ$         \\
4 & -0.0415 & $+12\,\%$ & $66^\circ$         \\
5 &  0.0000 & $0\,\%$   & $51^\circ$ ($=$ BDF5) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{NDF correction coefficients $\kappa_q$ adopted by cppDE,
the empirical step-size gain over classical BDF$q$ at matched
local error, and the resulting stability angle.}
\label{tab:ndf-kappa}
\end{table}

NDF5 is set to $\kappa_5 = 0$ because the BDF5 stability angle of
$51^\circ$ leaves no headroom for further reduction; NDF5 is
therefore identical to BDF5.

# Adams-Moulton coefficients

\label{app:adams-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} [@hindmarsh2005sundials], $\ell$-vector formulation
as in CVODE; cppDE implementation in
\texttt{adams\_set\_coefficients()} inside
\texttt{cppde\_multistepper.hpp}.

In contrast to BDF, the Adams-Moulton coefficients depend on the
recent step-size history and are recomputed every step from the
Nordsieck array. Define $\xi_j = (t_n - t_{n-j})/h_n$; the
$\ell$-vector recurrence reads
\[
  \ell_0(q) \;=\; 1,
  \qquad
  \ell_j(q) \;=\; \ell_{j-1}(q) \;+\; \xi_j^{-1},
  \qquad j = 1, \dots, q,
\]
followed by a polynomial expansion that yields the corrector
weights $\beta_0, \dots, \beta_q$ used in the current step. Because
the coefficients are step-size adaptive, no static table can
reproduce them in general; the canonical fixed-step values for
$h_n = h_{n-1} = \cdots$ are given in standard references
[@hairer2008solving], Table III.1.1 and reduce to the recurrence
above in that limit.

The maximum order in cppDE is $q_{\max} = 12$, matching CVODE's
default; the order controller may select any
$q \in \{1, \dots, 12\}$ at run time.

# Rosenbrock4 coefficients

\label{app:ros-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} [@hairer2010solving, §IV.7]; identical to the
default coefficients in the \texttt{rosenbrock4} stepper of
Boost.Numeric.Odeint. cppDE implementation in
\texttt{default\_rosenbrock\_coefficients} in
\texttt{cppde\_rosenbrock4.hpp}.

A Rosenbrock method of $s$ stages with diagonal coefficient
$\gamma$ is defined, with iteration matrix
$W = (\gamma h_n)^{-1} I - J(x_n, t_n)$, by the stage equations
\begin{align*}
W\, k_i
  &\;=\; f\!\left(x_n + \sum_{j<i} \alpha_{ij}\, k_j,\;
                 t_n + c_i\, h_n \right)
        \;+\; \frac{1}{h_n} \sum_{j<i} \frac{\gamma_{ij}}{\gamma}\, k_j
        \;+\; h_n\, d_i\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}, \\
x_{n+1}      &\;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} m_i\, k_i,
   \qquad
\hat x_{n+1} \;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{s} \hat m_i\, k_i.
\end{align*}
The cppDE parameterisation uses $s = 6$ stages with $\gamma = 1/4$.
The numerical values of all coefficients are reproduced in the
following tables, indexed exactly as in the source code:
the diagonal coefficient and the time partials and node positions
in Table \ref{tab:ros-diag}, the stage couplings $\alpha_{ij}$ and
$\gamma_{ij}$ in Tables \ref{tab:ros-alpha} and \ref{tab:ros-gamma},
the sixth-row weights in Table \ref{tab:ros-weights}, and the
dense-output coefficients in Table \ref{tab:ros-dense}.

## Solution and error weights

The advanced solution and the embedded error estimate are formed
from the stage values $k_1, \dots, k_5$ via

  x_{n+1} \;=\; x_n + \sum_{i=1}^{5} \alpha_{6,i}\, k_i,

  e_{n+1} \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{5} \gamma_{6,i}\, k_i,
\]

# Tsitouras 5(4) coefficients

\label{app:tsit5-coeffs}

\emph{Source.} [@TSITOURAS2011770], Table 1 and equations (7) and (8);

condition $\sum_j a_{ij} c_j = c_i^2/2$; the seventh
stage is the FSAL stage. Both rows of weights are listed beneath
the $A$ matrix: $b_i$ for the order-$5$ solution and $\hat b_i$

The seventh stage is $k_7 = f(x_{n+1},\, t_n + h_n)$, which is
re-used as $k_1$ at step $n+1$. Because $b_7 = 0$, the order-$5$
solution does not depend on $k_7$; because $\hat b_7 \neq 0$, the
embedded order-$4$ estimate does. The local-error estimator used by
the step controller is
\[
  e_n \;=\; h_n \sum_{i=1}^{7} (\hat b_i - b_i)\, k_i.
\]
The seven differences $\hat b_i - b_i$ are stored in
\texttt{cppde\_tsit5.hpp} as the coefficients
\texttt{e1}, \dots, \texttt{e7} and reproduced in
Table \ref{tab:tsit5-err}.

stored in \texttt{cppde\_tsit5.hpp} as

pair.}
\label{tab:tsit5-err}
\end{table}

The seven values sum to numerical zero, as required for the
consistency of the embedded pair, and the row $a_{7,j}$ of the
$A$ matrix coincides with $b_j$ for $j = 1, \dots, 6$, which is the
FSAL property.
